Don’t have a hearth or a pizza oven but love the blistery crunch of flatbreads and pizzas? Time to fire up the grill! Use the recipe or blueprint technique below to achieve the perfect grilled flatbread.

I’ve written about grilled pizza a number of times over the years (see my very old Serious Eats article here or my relatively newer NYT article here), and for good reason: For a regular home cook, grilling is one of the easiest ways to get the kind of intense heat that produces a pizzeria-style crust—soft and airy inside, crisp and blistered outside, with plenty of leopard-spotted char.

This is what I’m talking about:

And through I’ve written about the pizza technique, I’ve never really gone further towards presenting this as a more generalized technique for cooking flatbread on the grill.

Bread is one of my favorite things to cook outdoors. It’s fast, it’s easy (at least compared to other methods for making flatbread and pizza), it works with a wide range of lean doughs (even store-bought pizza dough!), it’s extremely forgiving (misshapen flatbreads are a good look that show you made it by hand), and on top of that, for many people who are used to grilled meats and vegetables coming off the grill, bread and pizza is a completely novel experience.

It’s also infinitely adaptable. You can make versions of classic flatbreads like pizza, lahmacun, naan, pita, or tarte flambée. You can use the flatbread as a base for any toppings your wild mind comes up with. You can use it as a bread for tearing up and dipping into olive oil, labneh, hummus, or other spreads and dips. You can serve it alongside a gorgeous salad and some simple grilled meat cooked alongside the bread. You can grill them and stack them under a towel to steam and soften into pliable wraps for kebabs, grilled vegetables, shawarma-style meats, or whatever else you feel like stuffing into it.

You get the idea. Pizza is just one branch of the family tree.

The Precedent

I started cooking professionally part-time while I was in college, but my first full-time job after graduation was as a cook at Cambridge 1, a grilled pizza shop and bar on Church Street in Harvard Square, opened by the same folks who opened Miracle of Science (the bar where countless MIT startups have formed).

There, we cooked thin, irregular pizzas directly on a custom cast-iron grill. The grate itself could slide toward or away from a hardwood-charcoal fire, giving us direct control over how much heat the crust was getting. I’d roll a piece of dough into a thin oval, drape it onto the grate, slide it over the glowing embers, cook it for about 30 seconds until it blistered on top and charred underneath, flip it, add the toppings, and grill the second side. The entire process took only a few minutes, and after mastering it at the restaurant, it quickly became one of my backyard cookout staples.

Folks from Rhode Island may recognize the concept of grilled pizza. The specific technique we used at the restaurant was taught to us by a chef who worked for George Germon and Johanne Killeen at their restaurant Al Forno in Providence, where modern American grilled pizza was created in the early 1980s.

But of course, humans have been cooking flatbreads—topped or not—over, under, or beside a live fire for millennia. That makes the case for thinking of this technique as a generalized blueprint for flatbreads, rather than pizza-specific, even stronger. The Science of Char

The underlying technique is essentially the same in every case: Take a piece of relaxed dough, expose it directly to the fierce heat of a grill, let it puff, blister, and char, flip it, then decide what you want to do with it.

So what makes it work so well?

Traditional hearths and pizza ovens fired by wood or coal regularly reach temperatures of 800°F (425°C) or higher. At those temperatures, a few things happen.

The first is oven spring. As soon as dough starts to heat up, pockets of carbon dioxide gas start to expand and water starts to convert to vapor. The result is a rapid puffing of the dough. This puffing all occurs within the earliest stages of baking (or grilled) when the dough is still moist and relaxed enough to expand. Once the crust gets set by heat, no more oven spring can occur.

Because of this, oven spring is highly dependent on the temperature at which the dough is cooked. Cooked slow enough, virtually no oven spring will occur as the dough starts to set and dry out before much gas expansion has occurred inside. On the other hand, pop dough into a blazing hot hearth or grill, and you immediately start to see it expanding and bubbling dramatically.

This oven spring is important to creating that light, airy texture inside the bread.

The second is a large built-in temperature gradient. What I mean is that with extreme heat, variations in cooking are amplified. So the tops of thin bubbles will get darkly charred while the rest of the crust gets crisp but stays lighter in color. Meanwhile, the interior is just barely set and extremely moist, having not had time to dry out.

The result is a thin, crackly, spottily-charred shell surrounding a moist, steamy, stretchy crumb. 

A backyard grill is one of the few common pieces of home equipment capable of approximating that kind of high-speed cooking, which makes it the ideal candidate for flatbreads as well.

And unlike a pizza baked to Neapolitan standards, grilled flatbread is remarkably forgiving. You don’t have to preserve a perfect cornicione around the rim. You don’t need a beautifully round skin. You don’t need an elegant launch off a peel.

All you have to do is roll the dough flat with a rolling pin, drape it over the grill, and flip it with a metal spatula or pizza peel. A few minutes later you’ll wind up with something beautifully puffed, charred, and crisp.

That’s what really makes this less a recipe than a blueprint. Once you understand a handful of basic ideas, you can take it anywhere you’d like. Both the blueprint for the best grilled flatbread and the recipe itself are included below. 

The Blueprint For The Best Grilled Flatbread

1. Start With Dough

The simplest dough to make is something like my standard Neapolitan-style pizza dough, although my NY-style pizza dough would also work. That said, virtually any relatively lean, not-too-sticky dough will work here. I’ve made naan dough with butter and milk that puffed and charred perfectly. I’ve made a quick bread-style dough using baking powder and yogurt that was perfectly pliable for wrapping around Turkish Adana kebabs.

For the simplest solution, just do what I did for the video: use store-bought pizza dough. It doesn’t crisp up quite the same way a homemade dough does, but it works perfectly well.

2. Get in Shape

The key to shaping dough in a way so it forms a great crust is to start with a very smooth dough ball. Honestly, watching the video above is the easiest way to see how I do this, but the basic idea is that you hold a 225g (1/2 pound) ball of dough by pinching just a little bit of it between the thumb and forefinger of one hand (think of it like forming a tiny outie bellybutton). Then with your other hand, pull the dough and stretch it over the top of itself and tuck it into the bellybutton. Give the dough a little rotation and repeat the process.

What you should end up with is a ball of dough that has a tight “skin” around it like a good ball of mozzarella. That skin should be gathered all into a little point at the base, which you can then smooth out by gently rolling the base of the ball around on an un-floured work surface.

3. Take a Rest

Every time you manipulate bread dough, you tighten its gluten network, which means that immediately after shaping, a ball of dough will be springy and elastic. If you try to roll it out, it will fight you, shrinking back toward its original shape almost as quickly as you stretch it.

Give the dough balls at least 2 to 3 hours at room temperature, covered so they don’t dry out, and the gluten will relax. A properly rested dough ball should look smooth, soft, and slightly spread out. More importantly, when you poke your finger gently into it, it should maintain that impression for quite a while.

You can rest dough in a specific pizza dough proofing container like I use if you make pizza often, or you can use small lightly oiled bowls or deli containers if not.

4. Forget a Cornicione

For most oven-baked pizzas, shaping the dough is partly about preserving bubbles around the rim so you get an airy cornicione. With a grilled flatbread, however, we’re not looking for a noticeable puffy rim around it (the cooking setup on the grill doesn’t allow for it anyway). This is good news because it means we don’t have to stretch our dough out by hand—a rolling pin will do the job just fine.

Moreover, you don’t need to worry about the shape. You can make a circle, an oval, a rounded triangle, an amoeba, or a blobfish. Whatever the shape, so long as it’s relatively thin and flat, the grill will take care of the rest.

5. Build a Two-Zone Fire

A two-zone fire is a grill in which one side is very hot and the other side is relatively cool. In practical terms, for a charcoal kettle grill(my grill of choice), that means you light a full chimney of coals and spread them under one side of the grill, leaving the other half empty. In a gas grill, it means turning half the burners on high and leaving the others off.

Now you have two tools in one: The hot side for cooking, creating the puff, char, and blisters. The cool side gives you control. By sliding the flatbread from the hot side to the cool side, you buy yourself a little extra time to top the pizza or let toppings heat up and cheese melt without the risk of incinerating the bottom.

That two-zone setup is the home-grill equivalent of the movable grate I cooked on at Cambridge 1. Learn more about setting up a charcoal grill in this video.

6. High Heat = Textural and Flavor Contrast

This is the key thing to remember with dough (or, in fact, virtually anything you cook): The faster it cooks, the greater the contrast between its exterior crust and interior crumb. At very high heat, the outside browns, chars, and crisps before much moisture can escape from the center. You get a thin, crackly shell with charred spots around a steamy, elastic crumb.

As the grill cools, the same dough will take longer to cook, allowing more moisture to escape and producing bread that’s progressively dryer and crisper over the course of a few bakes. This isn’t a problem. Both can be delicious.

But if you’re after that dramatic contrast, you’ll want to keep the grill very hot, which means adding some fresh coals to the top of the embers from time to time and allowing them to ignite before cooking the next flatbread.

7. Mise en Place Matters

As you’ve surmised, this whole thing happens very fast. Once the dough hits the hot grill, you have to start paying close attention to how its cooking and you have only minutes before it traverses from puffy and moist to dry and crackly.

Before I cook anything, I like to have my mise en place ready. That means having all of my toppings ready to go in separate containers with the right tools for spreading them on the pizza. It means having the dough, a rolling pin, some flour, and a surface to roll on ready and waiting. It means having my metal pizza peel (the best too for flipping and retrieving any type of flatbread) at the ready and serving platters on standby.

Once you start grilling, you don’t want to be searching in the fridge for the mozzarella.

Finally, if you want to take it one step further, you can pre-roll your dough balls in the kitchen before heading outdoors. Roll the dough balls out one at a time, dust generously with semolina, then stack them with sheets of parchment paper in between. It’s an easy way to make sure the cookout is all smooth sailing.

7. Draping the Dough: The Trickiest Bit

The only slightly tricky part in this whole process is draping the dough over the grill grates. Once the dough goes down on the grates, it’s very hard to adjust it until the bottom sets, which means that the initial drape will define the shape of the finished flatbread.

Luckily, shape doesn’t matter much. The only thing that does matter is ensuring that the dough is not folded over itself, and that its edges are not slipping through the grates closer to the coals.

If you have a round kettle grill, there’s another trick I’ve used for years: drape the dough initially over the cooler portion of the grill, then rotate the grate itself so the flatbread moves over the coals. You can rotate the grill as necessary to move the bread around as you bake and top it.

8. Grill and Flip

As soon as the dough goes down, it’s important to pay close attention and watch the bubbles forming on the top. Start peeking at the bottom of the dough after about twenty to thirty seconds, lifting them up with the edge of a pizza peel or large spatula and rotating the grilling dough as necessary to get relatively even browning and charring on the underside.

Once it’s nicely charred, you can flip the dough over and char the second side.

You’ll notice that the two sides have noticeably different texture, with the side we cooked first being relatively smooth but the second side being puffy and bubbly.

At Cambridge 1, that first, flatter side became the top of the pizza while the puffier side was underneath. This never sat right with me, so the one meaningful change I’ve personally made to the Al Forno/Cambridge 1 process is to give the cooked flatbread an additional flip before topping it so that the bubblier side faces upward.

9. Top as Desired, but be Careful!

Toppings are the biggest conceptual difference between cooking a topped flatbread on a grill and baking a pizza in an oven. A pizza oven surrounds the pizza with heat. Hot air and powerful radiation from above help cook toppings, evaporate moisture from tomato sauce, and melt cheese.

With a grill, on the other hand, the vast majority of the heat is coming from below. This leads to a few important rules:

Rule 1: Cook your toppings first. Toppings added to a grilled flatbread will heat through and herbs and tender greens may wilt, but they will not meaningfully cook any further than when they were applied. This means that if something needs cooking—say, mushrooms or sausage—it should be cooked before it goes onto the flatbread. 

Rule 2: Reverse your topping order. On a normal pizza, the sauce typically goes underneath with the cheese on top. For a pizza on the grill, since we’re heating mostly from below, you reverse that order, spreading the cheese (and not too much!) across the base of the flatbread before applying other toppings. 

10. Heat it all Together

After your flatbread is topped as desired, you can place it back on the cool side of the grill and cover the whole thing with a lid while you start rolling out your next dough ball. By the time the dough is rolled, the toppings should be piping hot, and you’re ready to cut and serve the first one (I like doing a rectangular party-cut for these) and get started on the second.

And that’s it. The perfect food for a backyard cookout or dinner for the family.

Whether you turn the bread into pizza or use it for dipping or wrapping, once you understand what the grill is doing—the rapid oven spring, the char, the crisp exterior and moist interior, and the fact that almost all of the heat is coming from below—you can stop thinking of this as a recipe for grilled flatbread and start thinking of it as a technique for making dinner.

A true wood-fired hearth may be the best tool for flatbreads and pizzas, but if all you really want is great flatbread—through any means necessary—there’s a very good chance the best tool for the job is already sitting in your backyard.

Recipe: Grilled Flatbread Blueprint

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • Once you master the technique, you open up a world of possibilities.

  • The heat of the grill delivers true hearth-style texture and flavor contrast in the bread.

  • The dough doesn’t need to be perfectly round, and a rolling pin works just fine.

  • It works with store-bought dough.

  • It scales well for a crowd.

Yield: 2 flatbreads
Active Time: 25 minutes
Total Time: About 3 hours, including resting time
Special Equipment: Rolling pin; charcoal or gas grill; metal pizza peel or wide metal spatula
Notes: Blistered, smoky, and crisp outside with a soft, chewy center, this grilled flatbread is an endlessly adaptable base for toppings, dips, and wraps.

Ingredients

  • 1 pound (900g) store-bought or homemade pizza dough

  • All-purpose flour, bread flour, or semolina, for dusting

  • Extra-virgin olive oil, for brushing (optional)

  • Toppings and dips, as desired.

Method

  1. Divide the dough into four approximately 225 g (8-ounce) portions. Working with one portion at a time, pinch a small bit of dough between the thumb and forefinger of one hand to form a little “bellybutton.” With your other hand, stretch the outside of the dough over itself and tuck it into that point. Rotate the dough slightly and repeat, continuing until the outside has formed a smooth, taut skin and all of the folds meet at one point underneath. Set the ball seam-side down on an unfloured work surface and gently roll it under your palm to smooth the bottom. Repeat with the remaining dough.

  2. Place the dough balls in a proofing container, lightly oiled individual deli containers, or lightly oiled small bowls. Cover and let stand at room temperature for at least 2 to 3 hours. The dough is ready when it has softened and spread slightly and an indentation made with your fingertip is slow to spring back.

  3. If using a charcoal grill: Light one full chimney of charcoal. When all the charcoal is lit and covered with gray ash, pour out and arrange the coals on one side of the charcoal grate. Set the cooking grate in place, cover the grill and allow to preheat for 5 minutes.

    If using a gas grill: Set half the burners to medium–high, cover, and preheat for 10 minutes. Clean and oil the grilling grate.

  4. Dust a work surface and one dough ball lightly with flour. Using a rolling pin, roll the dough into a thin oval, circle, rectangle, or whatever irregular shape it naturally wants to take, roughly 12 inches across at its longest dimension. Brush the upper surface lightly with olive oil if desired.

  5. Pick up the dough from one end and drape it oiled-side downover the hot side of the grill in one smooth motion, taking care that it does not fold over itself. Cook, watching closely, until the dough begins to puff and the underside is browned and charred in spots, about 30 seconds to 1 minute. Use the edge of a metal pizza peel or wide spatula to lift and check the underside as it cooks. Rotate or reposition the bread as necessary for relatively even browning. On a round kettle grill, you can also rotate the entire grill grate to move the flatbread over hotter or cooler areas.

  6. Brush the upper surface lightly with olive oil if desired, then flip the flatbread. Cook until the second side is puffed, blistered, and charred in spots, another 30 seconds to 1 minute. For flatbread you intend to eat plain, use for dipping, or turn into a wrap, continue cooking until it reaches your desired texture, shifting it toward the cooler side of the grill if it is browning too quickly. For flatbread you intend to top, cook the second side completely, transfer the bread to a tray or work surface, then top and return it to the indirect side of the grill and cover to heat through for a minute.

  7. Serve immediately or, for plain flatbreads, stack them under a clean kitchen towel to trap steam and keep them soft and pliable.

Bento boxes and bullet trains go hand in hand in more ways than one: Follow along as we enjoy a taste test and trace the history of these iconic symbols of Japan.

Content & Community Manager Erin here to introduce this episode of Kenji Eats Japan: Bento Boxes on a Bullet Train. Join Kenji and Akari to dive into bento culture and explore some of the common food offerings you might find at a Japanese train station. 

Bento boxes and bullet trains are two of the most iconic symbols of modern day Japan. But where did either of them come from, and how are they connected? Let’s dive in.

Bento Box History:

I’d argue, the evolution of bento boxes reflects the evolution of Japan as a nation. 

Their origins are simple and straightforward, with iterations of bento boxes appearing as early as the Kamakura period and continuing to evolve through the Edo period as an easy way to bring food to work, school, or cultural events.¹ It was during the Meiji era—a period of rapid industrialization and modernization that began in 1868—that bento boxes naturally took off in new ways. Modernization brought trains to the country and trains brought the need for food on long, steam-powered, locomotive journeys. This was the birth of “ekiben,” literally translating to “train station bento,” and from here, bento boxes were off to the races.

The evolution of bento boxes continued to hold a mirror up to society at large. In the wake of the First World War, bento boxes made out of certain materials became recognizable status symbols of your family’s wealth as the country grappled with economic turmoil. During the Second World War, resources that might typically be available for bento box production were redirected to the war effort, disconnecting the common citizen from this convenient delight. And in the post-war years, as school lunches were regulated across the country, they naturally fell further and further out of everyday use.² It was only in the 1980s with a convenience boom—as konbini, TV dinners, and the ever-helpful microwave thrived—that they came back in vogue, where they have remained since. For a deeper dive into bento history, check out this article by the Plenus "kome" Academy. ³

Today, bento boxes are more advanced than ever and, thanks to modern refrigeration and/or self-heating mechanisms, are able to serve more varied foods than ever. They also continue to be a popular choice for train commuters and tourists—like us!

All Aboard The Bullet Train:

Likewise, bullet trains tell a story about Japan’s evolution to the modern powerhouse it stands as today.

As Eiko Maruko Siniawer said in her book, Ten Moments That Shaped Tokyo, the 1964 Tokyo Olympics provided Japan with “an unparalleled opportunity to realize and demonstrate its post-war rebirth as a re-modernized, peaceful, and prosperous Japan,” but the Tokyo of the mid-century was a far cry from the city it became by the turn of the 21st.⁴

Physically, the city was in bad shape. The roads were rough, traffic was rampant, and the air quality was poor. The population was booming; the housing supply was not.⁵ Arguably too many things were made of wood (including outdoor trash bins which would, at best, attract pests and, at worst, help fuel the epidemic of catching and spreading fire that has forever plagued Japanese architecture.⁴) Though, to be clear, it wasn’t all bad: The country’s economy was booming and citizens were getting a taste of widespread, middle class ease for the first time, but it was decidedly not the bright screens, trash can–free streets, and clean sidewalks we associate Tokyo with today.⁶

This was no way to reintroduce Japan on the global stage, and, very practically, no way to move masses of people in, out, and throughout a metropolis hosting the Olympics. So, in 1959, ground was broken on the first bullet train (Shinkansen) line, leading to its debut just nine days before the 1964 opening ceremony.⁷ Originally, the Shinkansen went up to speeds of 130 mph (210 km/h). These days, they can reach over 200 mph (320 km/h) at their fastest and are relied on to transport hundreds of thousands of commuters daily.⁸

For the purposes of the JKLA team, the Shinkansen brought us from Kyoto to Tokyo in just over two hours, from Tokyo to Tsubame-Sanjō in just under two hours, and gave us a great excuse to grab some bento boxes and film a taste test while on the move.

Enjoy this episode of Kenji Eats Japan! And before I go: I want to extend a special thanks to Akari, Kenji’s assistant turned translator turned on-camera talent. This is her last feature film as part of this series and we’re glad you Frienjis love her as much as we do!

This blueprint recipe for do-it-yourself soup jars is perfect for back-to-school season and the chilly autumn months. Just add water!

Today’s recipe is a true blueprint in the sense that I won’t be providing any specific ingredients whatsoever. After watching the video and reading the article, I hope that you can come up with your own recipes using the flavors and textures that you love!

(And of course, you can still follow along with the video and make the Sichuan-style beef noodle soup, chicken and white bean soup, soba with tofu and egg, or chicken and hominy soup that I put together, or you can join our Cookbook Club to get these exact recipes later this week and test them yourself!)

Cup Noodles, But Make it Fresh

A little over a decade ago, I was poking through Hugh Fearnly Whittingstall’s excellent River Cottage Veg Everyday book and came across a recipe he called DIY Pot Noodles (“Pot Noodles” is is Brit-speak for instant ramen). The idea is simple: Fill up a mason jar with some pre-cooked noodles, aromatics, vegetables, and some sort of flavorful concentrated soup base, and you’ve got a fresh, just-add-hot-water lunch that is every bit as simple to prep at the office as a styrofoam instant noodle bowl, but far more fresh and delicious.

I loved the idea and immediately got into the kitchen to start playing around with it, seeing what flavor combinations I could develop and testing the best methods for stacking and storing various ingredients. At one point, a friend and I even entertained the idea of opening a kiosk in downtown San Francisco. You’d design your own soup or pick up a premade one, packed with fresh ingredients in a reusable jar. We’d sell coffee and pastries, too, so you could grab lunch while picking up your morning latte. At lunchtime, all you’d need was hot water.

I’m pretty sure I’ve recently seen a robot that does this exact thing at an airport. I guess an idea is only as good as the execution. I’m still open to investors, whether human or android.

In any case, I published four of those recipes on Serious Eats in 2014, including a kimchi and beef jerky noodles cup, a coconut curry shrimp version, one with vegetables and miso-sesame broth, and a super simple chicken noodle version with peas and version.

The noodles were a great starting point, but the method has turned out to be useful for a much wider range of soups. In the intervening years, I’ve started making versions with canned beans or tortilla strips. Rice cakes and tofu. Hominy or leftover rice. If it works in a normal stovetop soup, it works in an instant jar soup—you just have to know how to build the jar.

What follows is a blueprint for designing your own. Once you understand what each component does and where it belongs in the jar, you can put together or meal-prep your own lunches with whatever you have on hand. Let’s build one from the bottom up.

The Jarred Soup Basics

The most useful thing to remember is that the hot water is there to reheat, hydrate, and lightly soften the ingredients. It won’t stay hot long enough to reliably cook raw meat, dried beans, a chunk of carrot, or a nest of uncooked wheat noodles. Anything that needs cooking should be cooked before it goes into the jar. Vegetables you enjoy raw can stay raw, provided you cut them small enough that they heat through. Frozen vegetables—especially peas and corn which survive freezing extremely well—are typically blanched before freezing, which makes them ideal in this context.

Choose a wide-mouth container with a secure lid, large enough for a lunch plus the water that will turn it into soup. A one pint mason jar is a good small serving, but it can get tight. I find that these soup jars are kind of like burritos—our eyes are bigger than the container.

A quart-sized wide-mouth jar will give you more room to work, even if you’re only making a single serving. Use a container intended for hot liquids, and follow its temperature-change instructions; ordinary glass, including some storage jars, can crack when boiling water hits it straight from the refrigerator.

You’ll also want a small lidded container or reusable bag for what I call the “Flavor Pack”: the fresh toppings that get added to the jar after reheating. Think herbs, citrus, bean sprouts, nuts, croutons, and other crunchies and smell-niceys. When I first wrote about this method, I used small snack-sized ziplock bags for my fresh aromatics. Since then I’ve discovered a few options for reusable inserts designed to hold salad dressing under a Mason jar lid that work great for storing toppings.

Let’s start building those jars.

Step 1: Start With a Concentrated Flavor Base

Everything you put at the bottom is going to be diluted, so the base should be much more intensely seasoned than a finished soup. Powdered bouillon works just fine (especially for things like dashi), but of the dozens of supermarket brands I’ve taste tested over the years, Better than Bouillon paste is the best option I’ve tried (it also has a particularly high level of actual meat and vegetables in it). Choose chicken, beef, vegetable, or another flavor that makes sense with the rest of your ingredients, then build on it.

Step 2: Layer Flavors

Miso, sesame paste, chile oil, chile-garlic sauce, black bean sauce, hoisin or sriracha, a little soy sauce or fish sauce—anything you might use to season a soup or stew can all contribute flavor. 

Coconut fat or milk can add richness. A small amount of grated ginger or garlic can add bite, though it will keep more of its raw character than it would in a simmered soup. Canned chilies or tomatoes may be the right flavor for some soups.

Just remember: Whatever you add to the jar should taste good without having to cook it first.

You can also start with a concentrate that already has several of those jobs covered. Mentsuyu, the Japanese noodle-soup base made with ingredients like dashi, soy sauce, mirin, and sugar, is a good example. A tablespoon of canned Thai-style curry paste, chili jam, or shrimp paste will add massive flavor with minimal effort. Concentrated Sichuan-style hot pot soup bases (preferably the kind made with beef tallow!) are already designed for diluting and heating. 

Take advantage of it!

Step 3: Season

For a first jar, plan on roughly 1½ cups (350 ml) boiling water and use dilution instructions on your soup base as your starting point. Be aware that instant soup is typically extremely salty. If you want your soup to taste like it came from a college dorm microwave in the middle of the night, go for it. I won’t judge. But it’s always easier to start with less salt and season to taste at the end.

Ingredients like hot pot base, miso, soy sauce, jerky, and pickles can all contribute substantial salt, so make sure to adjust the amount of soup base you use accordingly.

Step 4: Add the Protein, Beans, Grains, or Hearty Veg

The bottom of the jar is the wettest, most highly seasoned part. Put ingredients here that can handle sitting in the concentrate, or that benefit from soaking up a little of its flavor. Shredded cooked rotisserie chicken or other leftover bite-sized pieces of meat, small pieces of ready-to-eat tofu, drained canned beans, and canned hominy are all good candidates.

Thin strips of citrus zest can go here, too. Think a strip of mandarin or orange with beef and hot pot seasoning, or lemon with chicken and white beans.

For meat and seafood, stick with fully cooked or ready-to-eat ingredients. Rotisserie chicken is especially convenient. Cooked shrimp, flaked cooked fish work, or even canned or smoked fish can work, as do small pieces of cooked sausage. Shred or chop everything into pieces that will heat through quickly.

Raw pork products like bacon or bits of sausage should be par-cooked before adding to the jar.

If you want things even more convenient, stick with dehydrated meats, like beef, pork, turkey, or salmon jerky. They absorb moisture and soften up while also adding flavor to the broth as they steep. Like making beef jerky tea, if that sounds appetizing to you.

Ready-to-eat fried tofu is particularly good at soaking up broth. A peeled boiled egg can sit down here, too. In a soy-based concentrate, the outside picks up some seasoning as it waits for lunch, just like the ajitsuke tamago you find in your ramen.

Think about this layer as protection for the ingredients above it. The wet seasonings stay low, the protein and other hearty ingredients lay a foundation, while the noodles and more delicate vegetables rest on top until you’re ready to boil them alive.

Step 5: Choose and Cut Your Vegetables

Choose vegetables for the texture they’ll have after a few minutes in hot water. The bonds between vegetable cell walls don’t really start to break down until just under the boiling temperature of water, which means that while green vegetables will get more vibrantly green and very delicate things like lettuces or thinly sliced onions will soften as the soup steeps, no significant cooking is going to occur. 

My basic rule of thumb for soup jar veg is to ask whether it’s something I could potentially eat in a salad. No? Then it doesn’t belong in the jar.

For firm vegetables such as carrots or cabbage, grate them or cut them into fine shreds. Slice snow peas and snap peas thinly across the pod. If you want to put in the effort, you can stir-fry or simmer vegetables that need more softening ahead of time, then chill and drain them before adding them to the jar.

Spinach and finely shredded romaine can go in raw. The spinach wilts, while romaine keeps a little crunch and catches the broth between its folds. Remove tough stems from greens and cut the leaves into pieces you can comfortably eat with a spoon or chopsticks.

Frozen peas, corn, and diced carrots are convenient and come pre-cooked as part of the freezing process. They can be added directly to the jar from the freezer to thaw while they wait for lunchtime.

Put sturdy or cooked vegetables lower down, over the base and protein. Save tender leaves for the top, especially if you want them to stay out of the salty liquid during storage. There’s no single mandatory order for every vegetable. The useful question is whether it will improve or deteriorate while sitting in the base.

Step 6: Add Noodles, Beans, or Grains

Just like with meat and vegetables, noodles will not cook in the jar, they’ll just get reheated. There are some types of noodles—very thin vermicelli, or shirataki noodles for instance—that can just be steeped before eating. Pre-cooked noodles from the Asian supermarket are also very convenient if you can find them. Otherwise, cook dry or fresh noodles according to the package instructions, drain them, spread them out on a sheet tray, drizzle with a little oil to keep them loose, then let them cool completely, tossing occasionally to make sure they’re coated in the oil. I like to par-cook and chill noodles in large batches, then separate them into nests in a muffin tin and freeze them. The frozen noodle pucks are the perfect size for my lunch or my kids’ dinners.

For a soup without noodles, use drained canned beans, lentils, or hominy, or a cooked grain such as rice or barley. These should already be tender. Unlike noodles, beans and hominy can happily sit right down in the base. With beans and lentils, you can control the heartiness of the soup by leaving them whole or mashing them in the bottom of the jar where they can later be stirred up to thicken the broth.

Just remember to go easy on the packing. A jar crammed with cold ingredients leaves little room for hot water and makes a lukewarm lunch. Leave space for broth, stirring, and the flavor pack.

Step 7: Make the Flavor Pack

This little packet makes a surprisingly big difference. Fresh herbs and aromatics can lose their freshness, while crunchy toppings like peanuts, fried shallots, or croutons lose their crunch as they steep in hot broth. Keeping them separate lets you add them at the moment you’ll get the most from their aroma and texture.

Think chopped parsley or cilantro, sliced scallions, thinly sliced fresh chiles, or radishes. A lemon or lime wedge lets you squeeze in the juice just before eating. Pickled ginger, capers, and other pickles can go here if you want them to remain distinct little bursts of flavor. If you want their juices to season the whole broth instead, add those to the base.

Tuck everything into a small food-safe container with a lid or a sealed snack-sized zipper-lock bag, then set it on top of the packed ingredients before sealing and refrigerating the jar until you’re ready to leave for work. These jars will stay good in the fridge for 3-5 days, depending on the ingredients used. (Dried or cured meats will last much longer than fresh ones like rotisserie chicken.)

Step 8: Store Cold and Add Hot Water at Lunchtime

At lunchtime, remove the flavor pack from the jar and top it up with boiling water. Cover it and and let it stand for about 3 minutes. If you want, you can lay a fork or a pair of chopsticks over the top the way you did with Cup Noodles as a kid so that the lid would stay flat while it steamed.

Stir thoroughly, reaching all the way to the bottom. I like to use chopsticks to break up any stubborn pockets of concentrate and loosen the noodles. Mashed beans need a good stir to spread through the broth, too.

Finish with the flavor pack, squeeze in any citrus, and eat.

The Basic DIY Soup Jar Blueprint

Use these as starting proportions and adjust after trying one jar. The weights of noodles, beans, vegetables, and proteins vary too much for a single interchangeable weight to be useful here, so in most cases, just use your own judgment. You know what you like.

Concentrated base: Enough to season about 1 ½ cups (350 ml) water, adjusted for other salty ingredients, plus your choice of complementary seasonings.

Protein: About ⅓ cup shredded or chopped cooked meat, cooked seafood, or ready-to-eat tofu; cooked egg(s); a small amount of intensely flavored jerky; etc.

Vegetables: About ½ cup thinly sliced, shredded, or cooked vegetables, loosely packed.

Noodles or another substantial ingredient: About ½ to ¾ cup cooked noodles, cooked grains, drained canned beans, or hominy; beans may also take the place of the separate protein.

Flavor pack: A few tablespoons of fresh herbs, scallions, or other toppings, with a citrus wedge if you like.

To serve: About 1 ½ cups (350 ml) freshly boiling water, adjusted to your jar and preferred consistency.

Spoon the base into a suitable heatproof container. Add the ingredients that tolerate moisture, followed by noodles (if using) and delicate vegetables. Put the fresh toppings in a separate packet and tuck it into the jar. Seal and refrigerate. To eat, remove the packet, add boiling water, cover, and steep about 3 minutes. Stir thoroughly, check the heat as described above, then add the fresh toppings.

Variations

The four soups in the video show how far you can take the same method. You can follow along in the video, or join the Cookbook Club for fully-written recipes:

  • Sichuan-style beef noodle soup: Beef base and hot pot seasoning, orange zest, beef jerky, noodles, romaine, and scallions.

  • Chicken and white bean soup: Mashed white beans and chicken base, shredded chicken, lemon zest, spinach, peas and carrots, and a parsley finish.

  • Soba with tofu and egg: Mentsuyu, fried tofu, a cooked egg, thinly sliced snow peas, and soba, with scallions if you like.

  • Chicken and hominy soup: A pozole-inspired combination of chicken base, ancho chile powder, garlic, shredded chicken, hominy, and cabbage, finished with radishes, cilantro, scallions, serrano chiles, and lime.

The older combinations I published over on Serious Eats still work, too: kimchi and beef, chicken and dill, sesame-miso vegetables, or coconut curry with cooked shrimp. Pick the broth you’re in the mood for, build a jar around it, make all your co-workers jealous. (Or be a real one and bring some for them, too.)

Deeply browned mushrooms, rigatoni, and a loose, glossy cream sauce finished with pecorino, herbs, and lemon.

I came across some beautiful chanterelles at Uwajimaya while filming our Japanese Pantry Guide the other day, and while I normally make this pasta dish with much less expensive mushrooms, I love chanterelles enough that I couldn't resist.

The good news is that the specific mushroom really isn't important here. Button or cremini mushrooms work great. So do shiitake, portobello, hen of the woods, oyster mushrooms, or virtually any mixture you can find at the grocery store or farmers market. The important part is giving the mushrooms enough heat and time to actually brown them before you start building the sauce.

This is one of those pastas where the sauce doesn't really exist until the very end. You start by browning the mushrooms hard in olive oil (I like to throw in a thyme or rosemary sprig while the mushrooms sauté and fish it out later), then add a little onion or shallot and garlic. Lemon juice gives it brightness, a tiny splash of soy sauce adds savory depth without making the pasta taste remotely soy-saucy, and chicken stock, cream, and butter form the rest of the emulsified base.

Now I know some folks are going to jump in and ask, “Have you seen that Cook’s Illustrated method where you start mushrooms in a dry pan to get rid of their water content before adding oil?”

The answer is yes, I have! And I’ve tried it! It works fine, but it takes longer and is more fussy that the traditional method of cooking the mushrooms with oil (which, by the way, drives out moisture faster than cooking in a dry pan). But if you enjoy that method, it’ll work just fine here.

The thing that actually turns all of these ingredients into a creamy pasta sauce is the pasta itself. I transfer it directly from its cooking water to the mushroom mixture, then cook and toss it hard and fast. Starchy water clinging to the noodles—and a little extra pasta water as needed—helps the fat, stock, and cream emulsify into a sauce that coats every piece of pasta without becoming heavy or gluey.

I finish it off-heat by tossing in big shower of pecorino and a handful of minced parsley.

By the way: A wok is my favorite pan for this. You get plenty of surface area for browning mushrooms and, more importantly, lots of room for tossing the pasta aggressively at the end (a large skillet works perfectly well too).

Recipe: Easy Weeknight Chanterelle Pasta

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • It works with virtually any mushroom, from inexpensive buttons to chanterelles or other wild mushrooms.

  • Browning the mushrooms first gives them much deeper flavor than simmering them directly in the sauce.

  • A tiny splash of soy sauce boosts the mushrooms' savoriness without announcing itself.

  • The final sauce is creamy without relying on a huge quantity of heavy cream.

  • The technique—finishing pasta directly in a loose sauce with pasta water—is useful for countless other pastas.

Yields: 4 servings
Active Time: 30 minutes
Total Time: 30 minutes
Special Equipment: Large wok or 12-inch skillet; medium to large pot for pasta; metal spider or other tool for moving pasta between pots.

Ingredients

  • 1 pound (450g) mushrooms, such as chanterelles, button or cremini, shiitake, portobello, hen of the woods, oyster mushrooms, or a mixture of the above

  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper

  • 3 tablespoons (45ml) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more as needed

  • 1 sprig fresh thyme or rosemary (optional)

  • 1 small shallot or ½ small onion, finely minced

  • 2 medium cloves garlic, minced

  • 1 tablespoon (15ml) fresh lemon juice, plus more to taste

  • 1 teaspoon (5ml) soy sauce

  • ½ cup (120ml) chicken stock

  • ¼ cup (60ml) heavy cream

  • 2 tablespoons (30g) unsalted butter

  • 1 pound (450g) rigatoni or other short tubular pasta

  • 2 ounces (55g) finely grated Pecorino Romano, plus more for serving

  • ¼ cup finely minced fresh parsley or chives

Method

  1. Trim the mushrooms as necessary. Leave small mushrooms whole and split or quarter larger mushrooms into bite-sized pieces.

  2. Heat the olive oil in a large wok or 12-inch skillet over high heat until shimmering. Add the mushrooms and thyme or rosemary, if using. Season with salt and pepper and cook, tossing or stirring occasionally, until the mushrooms have released their moisture and are deeply browned, 6 to 10 minutes depending on the variety and heat source. If the pan looks dry before the mushrooms are well browned, add another splash of olive oil.

  3. Add the shallot or onion and cook, stirring and tossing, for about 30 seconds. Add the garlic and cook until fragrant, about 15 seconds longer.

  4. Add the lemon juice and soy sauce and toss to combine. Add the chicken stock, heavy cream, and butter. Bring to a vigorous simmer and cook until the liquid has reduced slightly and begins to look saucy. Reduce the heat to low while the pasta finishes cooking (see next step).

  5. Meanwhile, bring a medium to large pot of well-salted water to a boil. Add the pasta and cook until just shy of al dente (a minute or two less than the package directions). Before draining, reserve at least 1 ½ cups (350ml) pasta cooking water.

  6. Using a metal spider, add the pasta directly to the wok or skillet, bringing along whatever cooking water clings to it. Increase the heat to high and cook, stirring and tossing constantly, until the pasta is al dente and the sauce is glossy and coats each piece, 1 to 2 minutes. Add pasta water a few tablespoons at a time as necessary. The sauce should look a little looser than you think it needs to; it will continue to tighten as the pasta sits and as you add the cheese.

  7. Remove from heat and discard any herb sprigs. Add the pecorino and parsley or chives and toss vigorously until the cheese melts into the sauce. Add more pasta water as necessary to maintain a loose, creamy consistency.

  8. Taste and season with additional salt, pepper, or lemon juice as desired. Serve immediately with additional pecorino at the table.

Hi everyone,

I wanted to take a quick moment to correct something I said in my latest knife-sharpening video.

In that video, I repeated a very common explanation of the difference between sharpening and honing: Sharpening on a whetstone removes metal, while honing on a honing rod merely realigns a rolled edge back into its original shape.

This is the explanation I was taught everywhere from other restaurant cooks and chefs, to my fellow editors and test cooks at Cook’s Illustrated and Serious Eats. It’s one of those things I’ve repeated so many times that I’ve never really considered that it may be incorrect.

So when a number of folks in the comments pointed out that research exists proving that honing does, in fact, remove metal from the blade, I went back and did some reading, particularly from an excellent website called Science of Sharp. The author has done a huge number of experiments using a scanning electron microscope to look at blade edges before and after sharpening, stropping, honing, and actual use.

And unlike a lot of discussions about knife sharpening—which can very quickly turn into people repeating things they’ve heard from somebody else—here you can actually look at the edge and see what happened to it.

It turns out that I was incorrect: Honing absolutely removes material from the blade, and in retrospect it seems almost obviously true.

How a Knife Dulls

If you are interested in knives, razors, sharpening stones, honing, stropping, abrasives, or just looking at extremely tiny pieces of steel, Science of Sharp is an incredible resource and rabbit hole to get lost in, and I urge you all to go there for the full picture, but for now I’ll offer a summary based on their research. There’s one article in particular called What Does Steeling Do? Part 1 that directly tests the idea that a honing steel simply realigns a rolled edge.

The first interesting thing is to look at what a dull knife edge actually looks like. The mental image I’ve always had—and the one I’ve presented in books and videos—is basically a very thin piece of steel that has flopped over sideways, bending, kinking, and rolling so that the sharpest bit of the edge (the apex) does not align with the direction of pressure. 

According to the microscopy, this is a thing that can happen, but it’s not the main way in which knives become dull through ordinary use.

A mushroom-shaped dull apex. Photo via Science of Sharp.

But according to the microscopy in Science of Sharp, it’s not necessarily the main way that knives become dull in ordinary use. In fact, there are a wide range of ways in which a knife tip can get dull. It can wear away through abrasion from cutting tough foods or repeatedly rubbing against the board. It can develop microscopic chips (or in the worst cases, visible chips) that make cutting rougher and increase friction. In some images, the malleable metal apex even gets deformed into an almost blunt mushroom-like cross-section at the apex.

What Does Honing Do?

None of these issues are ones that can be solved simply by “re-aligning” the apex and, in fact, what the author found was that in most cases, the work being done by the honing rod was not simply realigning existing metal, it was actually removing material at the microscopic apex to create a brand new cutting edge—one with a shallower angle than the edge the blade was originally sharpened to.

A cleanly rolled apex. Photo via Science of Sharp.

To further drive home the point, the author did another useful experiment. His goal was to test the effect of a honing steel on a blade that is simply rolled without any abrasions, chips, or major deformities. To do this, he used a glass beaker to push the apex of a knife blade sideways until it was visibly deflected, with a cleanly rolled edge you can see with the scanning electron microscope.

If there is any truth to the idea that a honing rod works by re-aligning a rolled knife edge, then honing this rolled blade should see the knife end back in close to its original state.

A freshly honed apex shown against a white outline of the original knife blade, proving that material has been removed to achieve a newly keen edge. Photo via Science of Sharp.

Instead, after using a normal ribbed honing steel, the edge is sharp again. And, instead of the original rolled edge simply standing back up, material has been removed from it, essentially creating a micro-bevel at the tip visible to the microscope but not your eye.

But wait. It goes deeper.

When Does Honing Actually Deform?

There’s a second article called What Does Steeling Do? Part 2: The Card Scraper which I think makes the whole thing even more nuanced.

If you’ve ever done woodworking by hand, you’re probably familiar with a card scraper. It’s a card made of soft metal that a woodworker will deliberately deform the edge of in order to create a little burr. This burred card can then be used to scrape the surface of wood creating a burnished finish that is smoother than anything you can achieve with sandpaper.

Looking at one of these cards that was very gently bent under the microscope confirms that indeed with light pressure, the steel bends and gets reshaped through plastic deformation, losing very little material in the process.

A card scraper edge showing the deformation as well as material removal. Photo via Science of Sharp.

However, as pressure increases to the point where it’s strong enough to create a properly-functioning burr on the card scraper, there is a combination of both deformation as well as material removal at the very tip. Turns out this is a good thing, as that material removal is what makes the very apex of the scraper—or the apex of a honed chef’s knife—actually feel sharp.

The Conclusion

The author’s conclusion is that burnishing can involve both moving steel and removing steel, depending on the pressure and the geometry involved.

So I think the final correction I would make to my previous explanation is this:

A honing steel can absolutely bend, burnish, or realign some deformed steel, but it is not accurate to say that honing merely realigns an edge while sharpening removes metal. Honing also removes metal, and in the normal maintenance of a kitchen knife, a large part of what a honing rod appears to be doing is removing a very small amount of damaged steel and creating or refreshing a microscopic bevel right at the apex. This appears to be true of ribbed steel rods, ceramic rods, and smooth steel rods.

There’s still a very useful distinction between honing and sharpening, and that largely comes down to scale. Sharpening on a stone works on a relatively large portion of the bevel. You are grinding steel away to thin the blade and recreate the overall geometry of the edge.

Honing works at a much smaller scale, doing much of the same thing, but only at the microscopic edge of the blade—the microbevel. And once you’ve used the honing rod enough times that the microbevel has been abraded or chipped past the point that it can be fixed, it’s time to pull out the whetstones.

I always love when I learn something I’ve always taken for granted is actually incorrect. It feels like a really great plot twist in a movie. The kind that makes you re-evaluate your past reading of situations and re-consider things going forward.

So thanks again to everyone who pointed me towards this really cool research, and I urge all of you to go check it out yourselves. There are a lot more amazing images and experiments to look at over there.

Grilling season has arrived and it's a good time for a refresher on the basics of setting up a charcoal grill. There are four basic steps you need to take before you can get started grilling.

Step one: Choose your fuel.

The most common options are charcoal briquettes or hardwood lump charcoal. Briquettes are made by compressing hardwood and sawdust into dense blocks. Because they're so dense, less oxygen can infiltrate them, leading to a longer, steadier, more reliable burn. Lump charcoal, on the other hand, is carbonized hardwood that moves fast and burns at a hotter temperature, better for high-heat cooking and searing.

Step two: Prepare your chimney.

With your fuel of choice, prepare a chimney charcoal starter. (I prefer this method to using lighter fluid or an electric starter.) These chimney starters are designed to circulate oxygen, moving heat up from the bottom to the top and slowly catching the coals on fire. After 20–30 minutes, the entire chimney of coals should be mostly lit and ready to go.

Step three: Arrange your coals.

I almost always establish some sort of two-zone fire. A standard two-zone fire would have all of your coals on one side of the grill with none on the other, allowing for a ripping hot heat zone for searing and an indirect heat zone for slower, lower-heat cooking. There's also a modified two-zone fire, which has most of the coals on one side and a few coals on the other for the same effect with a little less contrast. My write up on Serious Eats breaks down a few other coal arrangements you can try.

Step four: Clean and oil the grill grates.

Now that your coals are arranged, you can return your grill grates to their rightful home. I like to then preheat the grill for a few minutes, allowing any left-on bits to loosen, before cleaning the grates. No grill brush? No problem. These days, I actually prefer crumpling up a piece of aluminum foil into a rough ball and holding it with tongs to coarsely brush against the grates instead. (This also allows you to avoid the danger of wire grill brush bristles coming loose and ending up in your food.) Then, you're ready to oil the grates and start cooking. Do this a few times with 5–10 second intervals between, allowing the oil to polymerize on the metal.

Now, you're ready to grill! For even more tips on better barbecuing at home, check out my write up on Serious Eats.

A dull knife is both frustrating and dangerous in the kitchen. Follow these steps—along with the visual instruction in the video above—to learn everything you need to know about honing and sharpening knives.

Correction! After publishing this article, a number of folks pointed out that research exists proving that honing does, in fact, remove metal from the blade. I went back and did some reading of my own and issued a correction. Read it for free here or continue the original article below.

The other day I was slicing up some chicken thighs in order to turn them into tsukune (Japanese chicken meatballs, which you can find my recipe for here).

At least, that’s what I was trying to do.

As anyone who has seen that video knows, however, what was really happening was that my knife blade was slipping and sliding around on the tough, slick skin. The knife was clearly in need of a good sharpening, and that’s what we’re talking about today. But first...

How do I know when my knife is dull?

The first indication is difficulty finding purchase in a vegetable without either slipping off the skin, requiring excessive force, or deforming and crushing it instead of slicing. When chopping pungent vegetables like onions or garlic, you’ll notice much more moisture coming out of them and a stronger odor as cells are crushed instead of cleaved. Delicate herbs like basil or parsley turn dark and leave green marks behind on your cutting board—an indication of cellular damage and lost flavor and aroma.

The good news is that knives can be resharpened in a number of ways.

We’ll get to that too, but the even better news is that a knife usually doesn't need to be fully sharpened every time it starts feeling a little dull. The first thing to understand is the difference between honing and sharpening.

Wait, what's the difference between honing and sharpening?

As you use a knife, the very thin edge can gradually bend and deform. Imagine a line tracing along the very edge of the blade. In a perfectly honed knife, it should be a straight line with very few kinks. As a knife gets used, however, microscopic bends and deformities start to build up in that cutting edge. Rather than a laser-sharp straight line, it ends up jagged, tearing at food instead of slicing it.

By running a knife edge against a standard steel honing rod, rather than removing any material from the knife blade, all you’re really doing is straightening that edge out.

Note: After publishing this article, a number of folks pointed out that research exists proving that honing does, in fact, remove metal from the blade. I went back and did some reading of my own and issued a correction. Read it for free here.

How often should I hone my knife?

I hone my knife nearly every day. On average, I’d estimate that I hone my knife for about every half hour of total use—more or less depending on the demands of the task I’m working on. It may seem like a lot, but it’s an easy process once you get the hang of it, and the smoothness of a freshly-honed blade versus one that has been used even a little bit is noticeable.

Also, it makes you look like one of those badass butchers from movies.

(I’ve used my Wüsthof 10" honing steel for over 25 years now. You can get it here.)

What about ceramic or diamond honing rods?

Ceramic or diamond rods are not designed for honing. Because the rough ceramic or diamond dust coating covering the rods is much harder than the steel of the blade, it acts as a sort of very fine sandpaper, subtly shaving off material from the edge of the blade in order to expose a fresh edge.

These types of rods can be a good stopgap when you know you should probably be properly sharpening your knife soon, but you just don’t have the bandwidth to do it right now.

So, how should I hone my knife?

The key with honing is that you want to use smooth, even strokes, and not a lot of pressure. The goal is to gently coax the edge of the blade back into alignment, not to bash it into submission.

I like to hold the steel in my non-knife hand with the point facing away from me. I then run the full length knife along the full length of the honing rod, from heel to tip, maintaining roughly the same angle as the existing edge.

I generally do:

  • 8 strokes per side

  • 4 strokes per side

  • 2 strokes per side

  • A couple sets of 2

  • Then several alternating single strokes

The idea is to gradually work the larger irregularities down into smaller and smaller ones until the edge is straight again.

Test the knife on some actual food. If it cuts cleanly again, you're done. If it still feels dull, it may be time to move on to sharpening.

Do I actually need to sharpen my own knives?

No! For most people, the easiest solution is to find a good professional knife sharpener and send your knives out when they need to be sharpening.

There are a number of gimmicky tools out there that claim to sharpen your knives as well as a professional. Very few of them actually work as advertised. While pull-through or electric sharpener may put a decent edge on your blade, they also typically remove a large amount of material from the blade, shortening its lifespan.

Better are models that behave more like classic whetstones, gently removing material and maintaining the right angle in the process. Rolling sharpeners like the Tumbler come with magnetic guides that fix your knife at the right angle, and a rolling sharpening cylinder with multiple grits to fine-tune your sharpening.

But for the most control, you should stick with classic whetstones. It’s slow. It takes some practice. Even once you’re good at it, it’s an activity that takes time and patience.

Personally, I find that the time I spend with my knives and stones brings me closer to my tools, which makes me a better cook and my time spent cooking more enjoyable. (As I write this, I realize that this makes me sound like one of those guys who works on old-timey cars, or gains satisfaction from the way hand-carved dovetails just join together so satisfyingly.)

And while it's not particularly difficult once you get the hang of it, you are going to be using stones that can physically damage your knives if used incorrectly, so your first attempt probably should not be on your fancy $600 Japanese steel knife.

Okay, I’m convinced. What tools do I actually need?

A quality whetstone will last you for several of the lifetimes of your knives and fortunately, they are relatively inexpensive.

Like sandpaper, whetstones are marked with their grit level. The higher the number, the finer the grit. So while a 100-grit whetstone would be like running your knife over a gravel parking lot, a 10,000-grit stone is fine enough to produce a mirror finish.

The basic rule:

Lower number = coarser = removes material faster.

Higher number = finer = removes material more slowly and leaves a smoother edge.

To get started, at a minimum, you'll need:

  • A coarse or medium whetstone, somewhere around 400 to 800 grit

  • A finer whetstone, around 1,000 grit or higher

  • A stone fixer or flattening stone

  • Water

  • A non-slip mat or damp towel to hold the stone in place

  • A tray or cutting board to work over

  • A dedicated towel that you don't mind permanently staining with sharpening sludge

If you only want to own one stone, something around 1,000 grit is a useful compromise. For a more complete setup, I like starting around 400–800 grit for the bulk of the work, then moving upward. A 1,000-grit stone will refine the edge substantially; something like a 6,000-grit stone can polish it extremely fine.

And once you have your stones, you’re ready to start sharpening.

The steps to sharpening a knife.

After reading through the steps below, I strongly recommend watching the video above so that you get an understanding for hand position and movement.

Step 1: Soak and flatten your stones

Most whetstones are porous and can absorb quite a bit of water. When sharpening a knife, the goal is to always keep the sharpening surface completely wet so that the knife can glide along without catching or chipping.

In order to maintain that moisture, whetstones need to be fully submerged in water to soak until you no longer see bubbles escaping from them. It can take half an hour or longer depending on how recently your stones were used.

Once your stones are soaked, you can set up your work station.

I start by laying a damp towel on the counter and topping it with a rimmed baking sheet with a second towel laid on top of it. The tray is there to catch the excess water (there will be a lot of it), while the towels are there in order to keep the stone and the tray from moving. You'll also want a bowl of water nearby as you work so that you can continuously keep the stone evenly wet.

Step 2: Wet the stone and grip your knife

Once your station is set up, place your coarsest stone on top of the towel-lined tray. It should be oriented with the short side facing you (i.e., in portrait, not landscape).

Use your hand to splash water all over the top of the stone. The goal is to see the water completely cover the top of the stone without leaving behind dry or uneven spots. If the water doesn’t cover the surface evenly, you either need to soak your stones a bit longer, or you may need to flatten them using a stone fixer/leveler (more on that in step #8).

I grip the knife fairly firmly with my dominant hand, holding my thumb against the spine of the knife and my forefingers against the flat side of the knife. This position allows me to maintain some tension in my hand which keeps the blade nice and stable as I start to sharpen it.

The most important thing when sharpening a knife is the angle.

For most Japanese-style chef's knives, you're looking at roughly a 15-degree angle between the blade and the stone. Many Western knives are closer to 20 degrees. Either angle (or anything in between) can work for any knife you own, and rather than perfectly hitting 15 or 20 degrees, it’s far more important that you maintain consistency with that angle throughout the sharpening process.

Step 3: Begin sharpening

Start by setting the heel of the knife against the near edge of the stone at your sharpening angle. Now, while maintaining tension in your hands and keeping to that angle, gently push your knife straight up to the far end of the stone. Pull the knife back towards you at the same angle and repeat the process. At this stage, you should only be focusing on the heel of the knife—you’ll get to the rest of it later.

When I move my knife across the stone, I like to think of my forearms and hands as fixed in stone. Movement for the knife blade comes entirely from my shoulders and upper arms, while my hands are solely focused on maintaining the angle.

You do not need a ton of downward pressure, and there should be slightly more pressure while you are pulling the knife away from its cutting edge to prevent that sharp edge from accidentally slipping into the stone and chipping it. Think roughly of the amount of pressure you'd use when rolling a lint roller across your sweater and you get the idea.

Continue pushing the knife back and forth across the entire length of the stone around a dozen times, focusing just on the heel of the knife.

As you work, you'll see a grayish, silty slurry form on the stone. That's a mixture of water, stone, and material being removed during sharpening and will actually do a great deal of the work in allowing your knife to slide across the stone while gently removing material.

Step 4: Feel the burr

If you’ve been following the instructions or the video so far, you’ll have only sharpened one side of one small section near the heel of the knife. But it’s a start!

As you remove material from that one side, the very tip of the metal eventually gets pushed over to the opposite side, creating burr that’s so small you can’t see if with your naked eye—but you can feel it, and this burr is the best indicator that you have adequately sharpened that section/side.

To feel for it, gently run the pad of your thumb or finger from the side of the knife down along the blade (always pulling your finger away from the cutting edge, never along or into it!). On the side that you've been sharpening, your finger should glide smoothly off the edge. On the opposite side, you should feel the burr catch slightly.

Continue sharpening the same side of the knife, working section by section until you can feel that burr all the way along its length.

Step 5: Sharpen the second side

Your grip may change slightly when you reverse the knife, but the goal is identical:

  • Maintain the same sharpening angle.

  • Keep your wrist stable.

  • Apply only moderate pressure.

  • Put most of that pressure as you’re moving the knife away from its cutting edge

  • Work until you've created a burr along the opposite side.

Remember that the burr always forms on the side opposite to the one you're sharpening.

So by the time the entire second side has gotten a dozen or so strokes, it should once again feel smooth while that burr has now been pushed back over to the first side.

At this stage, I continue the same way I like to hone my knives: Keep sharpening it one side at a time, but with each flip, use fewer and fewer strokes until I am running the blade along the stone just once per side and the entire edge feels smooth with no hint of a burr.

Step 6: Move on to finer stones

Once you've established your edge on the coarse stone, move up in grit and repeat the process.

If you’re on a 400-grit, switch to an 800 or a 1,000. If you've just finished 1,000 and want an even finer, smoother edge, jump up to a 2,000 or 3,000. Keep going, using the exact same technique as you move up the grits, until the blade is as sharp and as gorgeous as you want it to be. Do note that as you move up in grits, the burr will become smaller and smaller—but your fingers are sensitive enough to feel it!

Keep reducing strokes as you finish, alternating sides until you're left with as clean and centered an edge as possible.

Step 7: Hone and test your new edge

You’ve probably all seen that classic paper test for knife sharpness: Run the edge of the knife at an angle against the edge of a sheet of paper and it should slice through it no problem. Personally I don’t find this particular test useful. Even a moderately sharp knife can make it through a sheet of paper but still perform poorly in the kitchen.

The best test for a kitchen knife is what it was made for: food! Grab something inexpensive that you slice frequently—an onion, an apple, or a carrot, for instance—and give it a shot.

Does the knife bite immediately rather than slipping? Can your knife slip through skin or shave off a paper-thin slice without crushing the food underneath it? Does it require noticeably less pressure than it did before?

If so, congratulations. Your knife is sharp!

Now please, just don’t stick it in the dishwasher.

Step 8: Clean, flatten, and store your stones

Once you're done, rinse your stones and flatten them as necessary. When sharpening a knife, you are essentially rubbing a curved object against a flat one. Over time, a shallow channel will end up forming in your whetstone, making it difficult to use without accidentally gouging your knife or stone.

The fix for this is a stone fixer/leveler/flattening stone. These hard, high-grit stones are designed to be run back and forth across the surface of a whetstone to grind away the damage and expose a new sharpening surface.

Once your stones have been fixed, rinsed, and allowed to air-dry overnight on a rack, they’re ready to go back into the dry closet until the next time you almost slice off your finger while cutting chicken—when the knife sharpening cycle can begin again!

I know I'll get some grief from the made-from-scratch bakers in the audience, and I'm prepared to take it with dignity and humility. Because these aren't really English muffins, they're pizza dough shaped and cooked the way English muffins are. But they're fresh, delicious, packed with craggy nooks and crannies, a heck of a lot better than what you buy at the supermarket and, most importantly, they're easy.

Traditional English muffins occupy this interesting middle ground between baked bread and griddled flatbread. Unlike most sandwich loaves or dinner rolls, they’re usually cooked almost entirely on a griddle rather than baked in an oven, which gives them their signature thin crust, tender chew, and soft interior full of nooks and crannies. A classic English muffin dough is generally wetter and softer than pizza dough, often enriched with milk or butter, and relies on a slow rise and gentle handling to create that distinctive texture.

If you're after a true English muffin experience, you can't go wrong with my friend Stella Parks' recipe from over on Serious Eats.

But for the rest of us who want to jump ahead without weighing ingredients and mixing and fermenting dough, I turn to pizza dough. Whether store-bought or leftover from a pizza night, leftover pizza dough might be one of the best “bonus ingredients” in the kitchen. It can turn itself into excellent sandwiches. You can use it to make pull-apart pepperoni garlic knots. And if you want a breakfast treat, you can easily turn it into English muffins!

Pizza dough makes especially good English muffins because it already has strong gluten development and long fermentation behind it, which means great chew, complex flavor, and lots of airy pockets inside.

The process is dead simple: Divide the dough into muffin-sized portions (about 3 ounces / 75g each), shape into tight balls, flatten them slightly, then let them proof on a cornmeal- or semolina-dusted sheet pan at room temperature overnight. Cook them low and slow on a dry skillet or griddle until deeply browned on both sides and cooked through.

Split them open, toast them, top with butter and jam, make breakfast sandwiches, or do what I do and stand over the counter eating one plain while the coffee brews.

And what do you do with leftover pizza dough English muffins? Why, make Leftover Leftover Pizza Dough English Muffin English Muffin Pizzas, of course. (I promise, that sentence makes sense).

Recipe: Pizza Dough English Muffins

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • Using pre-made or leftover pizza dough makes making craggy, tender English muffins easy.

  • An overnight rest lets you griddle the English muffins for breakfast.

Yield: 6 English muffins
Active Time: 30 minutes
Total Time: 6 1/2 to 12 1/2 hours (including the overnight rest)
Notes: Corn meal will give a crunchier finish to the exterior of the English muffins. Semolina will keep them softer.

Ingredients

  • 1 cup semolina flour or cornmeal

  • 1 pound (450g) pizza dough

  • Salted butter, for serving

Method

  1. Divide and Rise: Line a rimmed baking sheet or proofing container with parchment paper. Spread half the semolina or cornmeal in an even layer on top of it. Divide the dough into 6 even pieces, about 75 grams each. Form each into a tight ball. Space the balls out on the baking sheet then sprinkle with remaining semolina or corn meal. Lightly flatten each ball with a flat hand. Cover with a second overturned baking sheet or plastic wrap and let rest at room temperature overnight (between 6 to 12 hours).

  2. To Griddle and Serve: Preheat a large cast iron, carbon steel, or non-stick skillet over medium-low heat for five minutes, or use an electric griddle set to 325°F (160°C). Working three muffins at a time, lightly flatten them once more, then transfer them to the skillet or griddle using a spatula. Let them cook until the first side is nicely browned and the muffins are rising, 6 to 8 minutes. Flip the muffins, press down gently with a spatula to ensure the second side is flat, and cook until browned on the second side, 6 to 8 minutes longer. Transfer to a wire rack and repeat with the remaining muffins. Cooked and cooled muffins can be stored in a sealed container in the fridge for up to a week before toasting.

  3. To Serve: Split and toast the muffins and spread with butter.
