With over a year of testing and refining, the folks at Our Place and I finally built a grain cooker that can rice to the occasion.

Growing up in a Japanese household, rice was a daily staple, just as it is for my own family now. It's a rare morning when my four-year-old Wombat doesn't request tamago kake gohan (Japanese rice and egg bowls) for breakfast, which means that having hot, fresh rice that's ready-to-go can be a godsend.

Over the years I’ve used just about every kind of rice cooker you can imagine. The simple one-button models are easy and intuitive, but the cost of that simplicity is inconsistency: The rice comes out perfect in the middle, but a little mushy up top and slightly scorched on the bottom. The more advanced machines can make excellent rice, but they're often overly complicated or built with materials I'd rather avoid. For a long time, it felt like I had to choose between simplicity and performance. That's why the folks at Our Place and I have been working together on a rice cooker for over a year, designed to bridge that gap, and do so in style.

We wanted a rice cooker that is genuinely easy to use, but produces rice that is light, fluffy, and evenly cooked from top to bottom, with a size that is just right. With a great engineering team, thoughtful design, and over a year of testing and refining, we got there. (And I did the blind taste tests to make sure!)

I am so proud to introduce a brand new collaboration to the Kenji López-Alt Shop: The Our Place x Kenji López-Alt rice cooker. (Super Frienjis and Cookbook Club members even get a little early access discount code.)

If you’re interested, you can order from this link.

Grain Expectations

One of the things I cared about most during development was keeping the interface intuitive. My rice cooker is designed with just a few buttons that you don't really have to think about. It handles white rice, brown rice, and a range of other grains like jasmine, basmati, quinoa, farro, or oats. It also works well for simple one-pot meals—arroz con pollo, caramel apple bread pudding, even a frittata—without turning into a gadget that requires a manual every time you use it.

It also has a delay timer if you want your grains hot and ready at a specific time, as well as an automatic "keep hot" setting that will hold food at a safe serving temperature for up to 24 hours. On busy school days, I love that I can start a pot of rice cooking before bedtime, have it hot and ready for breakfast, and leave it in the pot hot all day to serve again at dinner.

There were also a couple of less obvious priorities that ended up shaping the final product:

  • It's made of non-toxic materials. It’s surprisingly difficult to find a rice cooker with a nonstick interior that isn’t built around traditional coatings, this one uses a ceramic nonstick surface made without PFAS, PTFE, or PFOA .

  • It looks great on the counter. Most rice cookers are designed to be stored away, but I wanted something that could live on the counter without looking like an afterthought (and something with a color and design scheme that would match my own Wonder Oven Pro).

  • It's extremely well-insulated. The walls of this rice cooker are significantly thicker than a standard rice cooker, which means that it heats more evenly and hold its temperature more efficiently, and ensures that any little hands don't accidentally get burned.

  • It's got great tactile buttons. This may seem like a small thing, but I love having nice clicky buttons on my appliances that give you feedback when you push them. Touch screen controls work great on ATMs and smartphones, but please, keep them out of my kitchen.

  • The capacity is designed for you. We took extensive surveys to arrive at the optimal size for typical home cooks. Six cups of cooked grains is big enough to feed a family, but not so large that it feels like a dedicated single-purpose appliance taking up valuable counter space.

  • It's easy to maintain. The bowl, the inner lid, and the sealing gasket are completely removable and dishwasher safe, making cleanup a snap.

Perhaps its most important feature is in what you can't see: It uses fuzzy logic technology to ensure perfect cooking every time.

Smarter Than Your Average Pot

What exactly is fuzzy logic? It's a branch of mathematics and engineering developed in the 1960s, designed to help computers make decisions more like humans.

See, computer chips are digital. That is, they think in terms of true or false, ones or zeros. A basic rice cooker turns on a heating element and runs until its single sensor detects that the water has been absorbed. It then switches off entirely. It's on or off, hot or cold.

Humans, on the other hand, are analog. It's not just hot or cold, we think on a spectrum. Very hot or sort of cold, frigid or lukewarm. So when a very experienced cook is making a pot of rice on the stovetop, they can fine tune the stove settings based on cues they're getting from the pot, gently reducing it once the water boils, for instance, or shutting it off towards the end to allow the rice to steam on its own.

Using fuzzy logic, our new rice cooker thinks and cooks like a human does. In fact, I'd argue that it cooks even better than a human. With its multiple sensors taking continuous readings, the Our Place rice cooker knows exactly what's going on inside the pot at all times, adjusting the heating element in real-time to ensure that the rice cooks perfectly.

It’s like the Terminator of kitchen tools: single-minded, relentless, and impossible to distract. It will not stop until your grains are perfectly cooked.

The Cooker I Rely On

It's been a long process, but after going through dozens of iterations (I have a full-on museum of not-good-enough rice cookers in storage) I finally have the finished cooker in my kitchen, and use it virtually every day. It's the kind of tool that looks great on the countertop, but it mostly fades into the background because I never have to think about it. It just does its job.

In pursuit of the perfect kitchen knife, we traveled to Tsubame-Sanjō, a world-famous metalworking region in Japan, with the help of some friends. 

Hi Frienjis,

It’s Erin, Community & Content Manager here with a special episode of Kenji Eats Japan.

So far in this series, we’ve brought you along to basement food courts and elegant tofu lunches, we’ve enjoyed Hokkaido milk flights and konbini taste tests, and we’ve made a whole lot of recipes inspired by our team’s travels through Japan earlier this year. 

But why were we in Japan to begin with? The story starts in Falls City, Oregon, and ends in Tsubame-Sanjō, Niigata Prefecture, Japan. Come along!

A Series Of Fortunate Events

A long time ago in a tiny Oregon town far, far away… 

Kenji met Gordon Hanson of Vonhelmick Knives by total happenstance during a road trip. Being a chef and artisan knife maker respectively, a friendship was quickly born, as was a beautiful knife partnership.

At Vonhelmick, all knives are hand-forged and just as Gordon’s steel supply started to diminish, luck struck again in the shape of a new friend, Eugene, who does a lot of business in Japan and wanted to help Gordon find a Japanese steel supplier. In the final link in this lucky chain, he eventually made the connection between Gordon, Kenji, and the family behind Aiba Steel. Then we were off to the races.

Working Together

Aiba Steel has been a family-run business since the Edo Period when their original hardware store opened their doors in 1861. Their business is guided by the founding principles of being kind and gentle, always being open to new challenges, and working hard to maintain the essence of their workers, partners, and local community.¹

Following in this tradition, the Aibas prefer to do business face to face. As their President Ryoji Aiba put it: “Building trust with clients requires more than just emailing or video calling… you should look at the other person in the face and shake their hand. That’s how you build trust.” This partnership bloomed over various trips to Oregon, a few stops in Seattle, and finally, a journey back to the Aibas’ hometown, Sanjō, in April of this year.

Tsubame-Sanjō is an area in Niigata Prefecture that combines the cities of Tsubame and Sanjō and is world-famous for its metalworking and manufacturing. There are over 5,000 small- to medium-sized companies located here and they host a particular fame for their cutlery craft, including some of the best Japanese knives you can get your hands on.² ³ In this industrial core, you’ll spot countless factories, foundries, workshops and forges. The roads are russet—a coloration they get from an actual coating of oxidized iron*, not a chosen, stylistic design choice—and the manhole covers are decorated with blacksmithing tools.

The devotion to their craft is etched, literally, in every part of the region.

*According to legend, the rust-coated streets come from airborne iron particles from the many nearby factories. The reality is a bit different, as it’s largely thanks to their sprinkler-based snow removal system that sprays warm water—which does contain higher levels of iron—across streets to help melt snow during the winter months. See their local train station above with the iconic rusty roads. ⁴

The Ultimate Hosts

While hosting the entire Vonhelmick (Hanson) family, extended JKLA crew, and business partner Eugene, the Aibas never wavered as the ultimate hosts. It’s hard to put into words the grace and thought they put into every aspect of our visit: Organizing multiple days of factory and foundry tours and activities to not only see different applications of their steel, but to really understand their metalworking culture; arranging chef demonstrations so our crew could gain insight to the local food scene; inviting us to get to know their business partners and, likewise, trusting us to share the story with all of you.

During our visit, we stayed in beautiful ryokans (inns) and were treated to kaiseki meals (traditional multi-course dinners) that featured impressively local and seasonal ingredients. Across three days, these courses featured everything from cherry salmon, rockfish, carp, and shellfish to snow-aged wagyu to seasonal vines, shoots, and bulbs. There were soup courses, tempura courses, and bowls of rice that were cultivated in the very town we stayed in. Every meal began with a toast of either non-alcoholic yuzu juice or a local sake and ended with a round of dessert and a cup of green tea. (Including my personal favorite: Build-it-yourself ice cream sandwiches with a selection of orange marmalade and red bean paste toppings and warabimochi and ichigo daifuku on the side.)

Through every tour, activity, and conversation, you could feel the attention to detail the family and their community put into their local industry. Through every ingredient and course served at dinner, you could feel the pride they have for their home shine through—and deservedly so. In fact, the minute I got back to Seattle, I headed down to Uwajimaya, our local Japanese grocery store, and bought some Niigata-grown rice myself.

Follow the Journey

We hope you enjoy this special episode of Kenji Eats Japan bringing you along to Sanjō with us. And stay tuned as the team gets to work making the next iteration of the Kenji x Vonhelmick Shi-Toku knife the best one possible.

— Erin, Community & Content Manager

Konbini are the cornerstones (quite literally) of quick, convenient food and drink throughout Japan. Kenji put the big three—7-Eleven, FamilyMart, and Lawson—to the test!

Hi Frienjis,

It’s Erin, Content & Community Manager here on Patreon with another episode of Kenji Eats Japan. This time, it’s a battle for the ages. It’s a Konbini Taste Test!

But First... What’s A Konbini?

Well, what does it sound like? Konbini is actually a shortened phrase for “konbiniensu sutoru” (meaning convenience store) in Japanese. It sounds similar to English because it’s one of many loanwords originating from English that the Japanese language utilizes, just like kurejitto kādo (credit card), eakon (air conditioning), or hankachi (handkerchief).

Convenience Culture

Japan loves a convenient food choice. Going into our team’s trip earlier this year, I knew the country had a big vending machine and konbini culture. The moment I stepped foot in Kyoto I realized, oh... they are quite literally on every block and every corner, sometimes in multiple amounts. The numbers back it up: Across Japan, there are around 60,000 konbini shops and 4–5 million vending machines (that’s one machine for every 30–40 residents)! ¹ ²

The vending machines come in all shapes and forms. Some sell your expected selection of soda, tea, and other sugary drinks while others might focus exclusively on coffee, beer, or even fresh-pressed orange juice. Some vending machines sell hot food and some sell frozen, microwavable meals so you can pop across the street and grab a dish for dinner or dessert. And while I didn’t spot any of these myself, some sell fresh produce, disaster relief items, collectibles, and more.³ And I’m not even including the gashapon craze in all this, though you can spot a fair number of those in the background of today's video!

While vending machines were surely part of our team’s travels—an ice cold Pocari Sweat is a great accompaniment while climbing a mountain to see some monkeys—we stayed focused on the konbini for the sake of this taste test.

The Big Three

Konbini are a cornerstone of the convenient food culture that’s endemic to this country. In 2025, convenience stores set a record ¥12.05 trillion ($75.8 billion) in sales, driven by the big three: 7-Eleven, Lawson, and Family Mart.⁴

  1. 7-Eleven is the biggest konbini chain in the country with over 20,000 stores.⁵ Yes, it’s the same 7-Eleven we have back in the States. The chain began in Dallas in 1927 but today is actually owned by the Seven-Eleven Japan Co., Ltd. parent company.⁶ In Japan, 7-Eleven is famous for their egg salad sandos and onigiri, amongst other savory food items.

  2. FamilyMart is close behind with around 17,000 stores and holds their fame in Fami-Chiki and comfortable sock stock.⁷ The Fami-Chiki is a juicy, crispy, fried chicken thigh kept in a hot case and served in a fittingly convenient rips-right-down-the-center wrapper to keep the grease off your fingers. The socks are self-explanatory, being cheap and comfy with a stylish colorway inspired by the store’s iconic blue and green logo. 

  3. Finally, there’s Lawson stores, with around 14,000 locations.⁸ They’re famous for their baked goods with affordable and incredibly high quality fluffy roll cakes, melonpan, and cheesecakes luring customers in. I only came across a few Lawson locations during my time there, which makes sense seeing as the areas we stayed in were FamilyMart strongholds (according to Conbini Wars).

Taste Test!

For this taste test, Kenji set out to try a variety of offerings from each store, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses. Our categories included egg salad sandos; onigiri; boiled eggs; fried chicken thighs (à la Fami-Chiki); socks; machine-made iced lattes; and a dessert wildcard. 

The results were not what we expected… Watch the full video for the taste test and beware of a spoiler alert for the final results ahead:

Thanks for continuing to follow along with the Kenji Eats Japan series! Right after we filmed this taste test, the team headed to the train station to catch a Shinkansen up to Niigata prefecture to begin the business half of the trip. Stay tuned for some super sharp stories about metalworking and knife making in Tsubame-Sanjō.

— Erin, Community & Content Manager

A skillet cake with jammy plums, buttery caramel, and a cornbread base that works just as well from scratch as it does from a box.

Hi folks. I've got a problem that perhaps some of you can empathize with:

Too many plums.

I know, I know. But server, my steak is too juicy and my lobster is just too buttery!

It's a high class problem to have, but there are only so many of Marion Burros' Original Plum Torte one can make. Luckily, that recipe forms a perfect blueprint for any number of excellent spin-offs using the same basic formula: Some form of batter topped with Italian prune plums and baked until the cake is set and the plums are jammy.

I've made this recipe using any number of batter from the excellent original recipe, to my brown butter cornbread, to a box of Jiffy mix. Honestly, use any type of mildly sweet batter designed to be cooked in an 8-inch square pan or a 9- or 10-inch round pan, and you are very unlikely to fail.

You don't need to stick to prune plums either! They are excellent because their high pectin content and slightly mealy flesh makes them turn nice and jammy as they bake, but any stone fruit will work, even (or maybe especially) if it's not perfectly ripe.

This time, I decided to flip the cake on its head—literally. Instead of topping a batter-filled pan with prune plums, I instead started by caramelizing some sugar and butter in the bottom of a 10-inch cast iron skillet. Once the sugar became a nice golden brown, I added a splash of lemon juice and water and simmered it down into a smooth, thick caramel. I then added the plums, cut-side-down with enough of them to cover the bottom of the skillet.

Finally, I topped the whole thing with a batch of mildly sweet cornbread (Northern style, don't @ me) and baked it until it was fully set. The one mildly nerve-wracking moment comes at the end, when you have to flip the whole thing out of the skillet. I do it by letting the cake cool a little bit and giving it a little shake. Once it slides back and forth a little bit, you know you're golden (or more accurately, deeply caramelized). I flip it out by placing a cutting board or cake plate on top of the skillet, then inverting them both together, giving the skillet a few taps to make sure the cake and all the plums come out.

It's excellent warm, or at room temp. With ice cream or whipped cream or nothing at all.

The new official JKLA World HQ Taste Tester-in-Residence, Ruby, agrees:

By the way, if you arrived here after picking up plums from us at the plum stand, welcome to the greatest community of food nerds on the internet. If you like what you see, you can join for weekly videos, recipes, writing, and other content delivered straight to your inbox. Check out our subscription page for information on the various tiers (including free)!

Recipe: Easy Caramelized Plum Cornbread Cake

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • It's virtually foolproof and works with a variety of fruits and cornbread recipes.

  • One skillet, one bowl, and great payoff.

Yield: 8 servings
Active Time: 15 minutes
Total Time: About 1 hour 45 minutes, including cooling
Notes: Italian prune plums are ideal here, but small plums or apricots work well too. Use any cornbread batter recipe intended for an 8-inch square pan.

Ingredients

For the caramelized plums:

  • 4 tablespoons (2 ounces; 55g) unsalted butter

  • 4 tablespoons (about 50g) sugar

  • 1 tablespoon (15ml) juice from 1 lemon

  • 2 tablespoons (30ml) water, plus more as needed

  • Enough small Italian prune plums, halved and pitted, to cover the bottom of your skillet (generally 6 to 10)

For the cornbread:

  • 1 batch cornbread batter sized for an 8-inch square pan, such as Jiffy, Bob’s Red Mill, or my brown butter cornbread.

To serve:

  • Whipped cream or ice cream

Method

  1. Adjust an oven rack to the middle position and preheat oven to 350°F (175°C).

  2. Combine butter and sugar in a 10-inch cast iron, carbon steel, or oven-safe nonstick skillet. Cook over medium heat, stirring and swirling occasionally, until the butter is melted and the sugar begins to caramelize and turn golden brown.

  3. Add the lemon juice and water all at once (the sugar will sputter aggressively) and immediately start swirling the pan and stirring the mixture over heat until the sugar is completely dissolved. You may need to add more water if it is evaporating too aggressively. Add it a tablespoon at a time until the sugar melts smoothly.

  4. Continue cooking the caramel until a spatula scraped across the bottom of the pan leaves a trail that slowly closes. Remove the skillet from heat. Arrange the plum halves snugly in the caramel, cut-sides-down.

  5. Prepare your cornbread batter according to its recipe or package directions. Butter the sides of the skillet, then pour the batter evenly over the plums and gently spread it to the edges using a spatula. Some of the caramel is likely to ride up the edges or swirl into the middle. This is OK.

  6. Transfer skillet to oven and bake until the cornbread is golden brown and a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean, about 50 minutes (start checking after 45 minutes).

  7. Remove skillet from oven. Give it a gentle shake to make sure the cake has released from the sides and bottom, then let cool in the skillet for at least 10 minutes.

  8. Place a large cake platter or cutting board upside down over the skillet. Holding the platter and skillet firmly together, invert them in one confident motion. Carefully lift off the skillet. If any plums stuck to the bottom of the skillet, carefully lift them out and replace them on the cake.

  9. Cut into wedges and serve warm or at room temperature with whipped cream or ice cream.

Daughter of the Phở Bắc family, Yenvy stopped by to chat with Kenji about how her parents established their roots in Seattle’s Little Saigon neighborhood while carrying forward the bold, bright flavors of Vietnam.

If you’re not a local, you might not know that Seattle has really, really good pho—and that is largely thanks to the family behind Phở Bắc.

The first pho restaurant in the city was actually not a pho restaurant at all. Cat’s Submarine Sandwich Shop was established by Vietnamese refugees, Theresa Cat Vu and Augustine Nien Pham, who were urged and eventually convinced by their community in the Little Saigon neighborhood to start selling the soup staple. It was an instant hit and the restaurant was renamed shortly after to Phở Bắc. (IYKYK: This building is known to locals today as “The Boat.”)

Since 1982, Phở Bắc has expanded into a family of restaurants throughout the city. Now, the business is run by the second generation of Phams, sisters Yenvy and Quynh-vy, who have a book coming out this fall called Phởnomenal Nights which will feature bright, bold Vietnamese flavors and meals meant for sharing.

A few months ago, Yenvy stopped by Kenji’s kitchen to talk about the book, Vietnamese cuisine, and her family’s history—all while they made a mean crab dip. Now, I’ll let Kenji and Yenvy take it away!

— Erin, JKLA World HQ Community Manager

The following quotes are edited and condensed for flow from Kenji and Yenvy's full conversation. For more, watch the video above or on YouTube.

The Dishes Behind Phởnomenal Nights

Yenvy: The book is very Vietnamese-American because, you know, I was born and raised in Seattle. This crab dip is obviously a mix. It’s American with some Vietnamese flavors or influence. In the book, there’s also a lot of soups; things like a roasted chicken for two and skewers with shrimp paste; a whole chapter on sauces (there’s a lot of sauces—my editor was like, “You have twenty different sauces in here?!”); and a big pickle section at the start. My sister did all the cocktails, and I did all the food.

Kenji: How much of this kind of stuff do you consider when making a menu or recipes for a book: Do you think about what’s authentically Vietnamese versus not, or what’s uniquely yours versus how much you need to maintain some sort of tradition?

Yenvy: The first thing I think about when I make a dish is: “Do you crave it?” For me, my palate just loves Vietnamese food the most, so I’m motivated and inspired by our cuisine and don’t really think about it being authentic because, what does that mean anyways? But I bring the flavors of Vietnamese food—it tastes like Vietnam, you know. And even for Vietnamese people, it can be something they’re not used to or haven’t had before, but they still find it satisfying. Lots of it can be different variations of the same stuff. Like, even the dry noodle at the súp shop or the rice dish at The Boat. Everything familiar is there, but it’s not what people would usually blend or mix.

Kenji: Then when you’re making a new dish, what’s the last step you go through before you’re done?

Yenvy: I have to hate it. So, I’ll make the recipe and try it out and think it’s good. Then I have to revisit it later to see if it’s actually good. And I’ll have everyone taste it, so my sister will be there too.

If someone bought your book, what are the five pantry staples they need?

Yenvy: Fish sauce. Fish sauce. Everything has fish sauce. Fried shallots—I have a massive jar of fried shallots because they go into everything. They make everything better.

Kenji: Is it okay for people to buy those, or must you make them?

Yenvy: You must make them. You could use yellow onions, too, but it’s such an essential thing you’ll probably want shallots. If you buy them, you can go to Vietnamese delis—or Vietnamese grocery stores, which always have a deli—and get them fresh.

I also like sugar. Vietnamese food has a lot of sugar. I cook a lot with honey, and always have that or brown sugar around. It can be any type of sugar, really. I just feel healthier when I use honey.

[Another staple] is Maggi seasoning. So, fish sauce, fried shallots, sugar, Maggi, and then an acid, like vinegar. I either use a simple distilled vinegar or rice wine vinegar. Anything neutral in flavor. That’s a good five staples.

The Essentials in Vietnamese Cuisine

Kenji: What are the things that really make Vietnamese food to you—what are the distinctive elements? Is it a flavor thing? The way you eat it and the experience of eating it and how it’s served? The type of dishes you’re making?

Yenvy: I think it's definitely the flavor. Vietnamese cuisine is really about hitting all the notes. Like, you have the salty, the sweet, the sour, the bitter, the umami, and the herbs. We put herbs in everything (...and fried shallots). Fresh herbs, anything really fresh.

And it can be the way we eat it sometimes, like there are individual dishes you eat alone then the shareable dishes. Vietnamese cuisine is about satisfying all of your palates. We want a little soup, a little dry, a little saucy, and lots of different textures. Especially chewy stuff.

Kenji: That’s one of the things that I find sort of distinctive about a lot of Asian cuisines; chewy is not really something people tend to like in the U.S. Chewy, slippery, and gelatinous are things Japanese, Chinese, Vietnamese people really like. But if you describe something like that on an American menu, [lots of] people would go crazy.

Leaving Vietnam

Kenji: Tell me about how your parents came here from Vietnam. It’s a pretty wild story, to my understanding.

Yenvy: Oh, it’s so crazy. They didn’t get out until their fourth attempt. So, [going back] my parents fled two wars. First in 1945 from northern Vietnam to southern Vietnam when they were both under twelve years old. That’s why the restaurant is called Phở Bắc, because they have a lot of northern pride. (Phở Bắc means northern-style pho.) But my mom’s palate is hella southern, while northern food tends to be milder.

My dad had a coffee shop back in the day in Vietnam and, when my parents lost the coffee shop in '75, he went to make tires after one of the deacons at the church taught him how. They started manufacturing tires in Saigon and then my dad had money during, you know, the fall and disarray of the country. He paid to try to get them out of Vietnam but was taken advantage of and they got robbed the first three attempts and eventually got caught and thrown in jail. My dad was in there for a year but my mom was let go once Quynh, my older sister, was born.

They finally made it out onto sea and they were out there for twelve days. They got robbed by pirates—everything was lost—then the motor died and they were just drifting. My aunt, who was on the boat, then saw a fishing boat. At the time, if you brought in refugees, you got thrown in jail so this Thai fisherman told them to swim to shore but my mom, who’s a very audacious woman, was like, “I’m not swimming with these children! I’m going to drown!” She was so adamant that he felt bad and pulled them to shore and got arrested. We don’t know what happened to them. It’s such a crazy story. From there, they went to the Philippines and got sponsored over to Seattle by my aunt.

Arriving in Seattle

Yenvy: Near the church right next to Little Saigon, my parents saw this little 600-square-foot building on the corner for lease. My parents were both natural-born entrepreneurs so they were like, let’s open a restaurant! It started off as a sub shop because my mom thought, you know, that’s what Americans wanted.

Kenji: What year was this? Were there Vietnamese restaurants already?

Yenvy: This was 1982. We had the grocery store, Viet-Wah, where everyone went shopping, we had a temple, and probably two restaurants—so all the Vietnamese people lived around here. Anyways, my mom ran the sub shop but, on the weekends, everyone told her how she needed to make pho. She threw a lot of dinner parties and everyone knew her for her pho. Next thing you know, [at the shop] everyone wanted pho and the subs became obsolete.

Kenji: When your parents first came to Seattle, did they immediately find a community here?

Yenvy: Oh, yes. So my aunt—she also has a pho shop called Crazy Pho Cajun in Federal Way—she had already come here by getting sponsored by a nice white family. And the church was already established and the community was hyper-social so they always had gatherings and they were super tight.

Uplifting Little Saigon

Kenji: What were your parents' feelings on building and maintaining the community? Cause I know you and your sister do a lot of work advocating for and building and maintaining the Vietnamese community in Little Saigon. Was that something that was important to them as well?

Yenvy: Yeah, they were super involved. They knew everyone. My parents, I think they sponsored over 150 families to move here. So growing up there were always people in my house I didn’t know. I was just like, “just another day!” They were always really big on community building and the community was thriving.

Right now [with the work I’m doing], I’m not trying to capture nostalgia. It’s more like, what’s next? With our neighborhood, we’re trying our best. And I can only control what I can, so it’s more about activation. My solution to everything is getting people to want to be in the neighborhood, including goods and services.

We have the nonprofit Friends of Little Saigon and now we have this $70 million dollar project called the Landmark Project going into the neighborhood—that’s going to be the anchor of everything. We break ground in September. It will be multifamily housing, a community center, and a gathering space for arts and culture. I’ll also be moving Hello Em over as an anchor tenant and Trinh (owner of Bainbridge’s Ba Sa and Capitol Hill’s Ramie restaurants) is gonna open her micro-pastry shop in there, too.

Kenji: And your parents, are they still with us?

Yenvy: Oh yeah! We all live within a mile of each other or less. They retired like 20 years ago—they’re too busy gardening now!

Learning to make a simple emulsion of fat, pasta water, and cheese opens the gates to a host of other dishes (pasta and beyond), and this pasta alla gricia is the easiest way to learn it.

“So, basically, spaghetti with scrambled eggs and bacon?” I asked.

“Assolutamente NO! Macché!” shouted Carolina. “Carbonara is silky and smooth and we use guanciale, not this stuff you call bacon, and we have real cheese and better pasta and we just know how to do it.”

Yes, Carolina was Roman, and yes, she was proud of her city’s pasta dishes.

I was 19, and this was the first time I had heard about pasta carbonara, much less tried to make it. Of course, being the completely green and overly confident cook that I was at that age, I mucked it up completely. Hence, scrambled eggs and bacon.

In truth, there’s no secret to making perfect versions of the four big Roman pasta dishes. It just takes a little know-how and technique.

If you’re lucky, you already learned this technique in your family’s kitchen, absorbing it as you grew up until, by now, it’s second nature. But for the rest of you, read on.

Roman Pasta DNA

At their heart, the sauces for the four major Roman pasta dishes—pasta cacio e pepe, pasta alla gricia, pasta carbonara, and pasta all’amatriciana—are all simple emulsions of fat and water with varying amounts and kinds of protein in the mix.

I like to think of them as a family tree:

  • Cacio e Pepe is the simplest with pasta water, grated sheep’s milk cheese, and black pepper.

  • Pasta alla Gricia is like cacio e pepe, but with the addition of cured pork, typically guanciale that is cooked in the pan to release rendered fat that emulsifies into the sauce.

  • Pasta Carbonara is like pasta alla gricia with the addition of eggs, which turn the sauce richer and more velvety.

  • Pasta all’Amatriciana is pasta alla gricia with the addition of tomatoes (and, if you want to start a fight with a Roman, onions).

If you want to master all four of these pastas, I’d suggest starting with alla gricia, which is what we’re talking about today. It still teaches you the very basics of forming an emulsified pan sauce, but is more forgiving than eacio e pepe, which has a tendency to clump if you are not very careful with temperatures.

And once you’ve mastered this one, you can hit up cacio e pepe, carbonara, and amatriciana with confidence. (Stay tuned for updates on all those recipes coming soon.) Not only that, but you’ll now have the skills to:

  • Make glossy pan sauces for chicken, fish, or pork chops

  • Properly finish any pasta dish so the sauce clings instead of drips

  • Glaze carrots, peas, or other vegetables until shiny and lacquered

  • Mount butter into sauces without breaking them

  • Understand why some sauces turn greasy while others become silky and unified

  • Improvise confidently instead of relying strictly on recipes

Sound good?

The Science of Silkiness

Fat and water need a little help getting along.

So what exactly is an emulsion?

Well, like my old cat Pike and my old dog Dumpling, fat and water are chemically disinclined to mingle. Water molecules are polar, while fat molecules are non-polar and, as a general rule, these molecules like to stick with their own kind, like '80s kids at a middle school dance. Left alone, oil and water separate into distinct layers because that’s the most stable, lowest energy arrangement available to them.

An emulsion is what happens when one liquid is broken into droplets that are tiny enough that they can be evenly dispersed throughout another liquid. These tiny droplets move more slowly and collide less energetically, making it much harder for them to coalesce back into separate oil and water phases. This dispersion also causes the entire mixture to turn more viscous. 

The problem is that emulsions are naturally unstable, and most of them will be temporary unless we add something to help them keep together. In mayonnaise, that stabilizer is lecithin found in the egg yolk—a molecule with the ability to bridge the gap between polar and non-polar molecules. In a dijon vinaigrette, that stabilizer is the natural gums, fine particles, and surface-active compounds found in mustard seeds or garlic that both thicken the liquid and help keep droplets apart. And In Roman pasta dishes, that stabilizer is starch.

As pasta cooks, it releases starch molecules into the water. Those starches swell up, thickening the liquid and further interfering with the tiny fat droplets’ ability to coalesce. This helps suspend everything together into a glossy sauce instead of a greasy puddle.

This is why pasta water matters so much, and why the pasta you order at 8:00pm is probably better than the pasta you order at 5:30pm when the restaurant opens.

Let me explain.

The Secret Ingredient is In the Room

And it’s been swirling around in the pasta pot this whole time.

You see, when I worked pasta station professionally, we cooked our pasta in a giant 15-gallon recirculating pasta boiler with six baskets constantly dropping pasta throughout service. Early in the night, the water was relatively clear. By the end of service, it had become cloudy and thick with dissolved starch.

And the pasta got better as the night went on.

Late-night sauces emulsified more easily, clung to noodles more beautifully, and looked silkier and glossier. The starchier the water became, the easier it was to form stable emulsions. That experience permanently changed how I cook pasta at home.

The Best Pasta is Rough Around the Edges

Texture matters on a microscopic level.

First, let’s talk about choosing the right dried pasta (these Roman pasta dishes are almost always made with dried pasta), which matters more than you may realize. This is one of those cases where the shape matters, but the surface matters even more.

Old school Italian dried pasta is extruded through bronze dies, which give the noodles a slightly rough, chalky, almost dusty-looking exterior. Modern industrial pasta is often extruded through Teflon dies instead, producing noodles with a smoother, shinier, almost plasticky surface. That smoother surface looks sleek, but it gives sauce very little to cling to. Bronze-die pasta, by contrast, has microscopic ridges, pits, and irregularities that dramatically increase surface area and create countless little nooks for sauce to grab onto.

 When you build an emulsified sauce like alla gricia—where rendered pork fat, starchy water, and cheese are suspended together into a glossy glaze—that rough surface helps the sauce coat the pasta evenly instead of sliding off and pooling in the bottom of the bowl.

Bronze-die pasta also tends to shed starch more readily into the cooking water, and that matters just as much as texture. That extra starch is liquid gold in Roman pasta cooking; it thickens the water, stabilizes the emulsion, and helps bind fat and cheese into a silky sauce that clings to every noodle. In other words, bronze-die pasta improves both halves of the equation: it gives you better sauce in the pan, and it gives that sauce a better surface to cling to on the plate.

Big Pot Energy

Are giant pasta pots the right choice?

What about the way we cook it?

Traditional pasta advice says to use a huge pot with at least a gallon of water per pound of pasta. But for the vast majority of cases, that’s actually counterproductive. More water dilutes the starch. Less water concentrates it. And concentrated starch means a more stable emulsion.

I can hear folks getting their fingers ready to type, "But I learned that a larger pot returns to a boil faster, and that’s important for the perfect pasta texture!"

That’s mostly kitchen myth.

For one thing, a small pot will actually return to a boil faster than a large pot when you add pasta to it.  When you add pasta (or asparagus, or frozen peas, or spinach, or anything) to a pot of boiling water, the thing cooling the pot down is the pasta itself. So the energy required to bring the system back to a boil is simply the amount of energy needed to heat that pasta up to boiling temperature. So whether the pasta is sitting in one quart of water or three gallons of water, the pot still requires the exact same amount of energy to return to a boil.

In this perfectly insulated system, small and large pots would return to a boil at the exact same rate.

But real kitchens aren’t perfectly insulated. Heat escapes into the room and steam carries energy away. Because of their larger surface areas, larger pots actually lose more heat to the kitchen than small pots. So in practice, smaller pots actually return to a boil slightly faster, not slower.

TL;DR: The pasta cooks just as well in a small pot, and the water comes out starchier, which makes emulsions easier.

Pasta Bullet Time

Slow cooking in the fast lane.

With pasta dishes, I virtually always pull the pasta out of the water and add it to the pan of sauce along with whatever pasta water is clinging to it when it is still a couple minutes short of al dente—while the center is still a little chalky in texture. In the case of pasta alla gricia, that pan sauce is simply crisply rendered chunks of guanciale or pancetta and the fat they’ve given off, along with some black pepper.

By finishing the pasta in the sauce, you take advantage of something my friend Daniel Gritzer refers to as “pasta bullet time": once pasta leaves rapidly boiling water and enters the skillet, cooking slows down significantly. What would have taken another two minutes in the pot might take four or five minutes in the pan.

That slower finishing period is an advantage. By adding a little splash of pasta water occasionally as the pan needs it, you can ensure that the sauce comes into perfect emulsion at the same time as the pasta finishes cooking, while also building extra flavor into the pasta itself. How do you know when to add pasta water? If the sauce starts to look too thick, or it breaks and looks greasy, that’s your sign. Splash pasta water into the pan and let it reduce again until emulsified.

Incidentally, you should always make these types of pan sauces over high heat. The rapid bubbling physically helps disperse fat droplets through the water phase of the sauce and actively strengthens the emulsion.

Case In Point

The other enemy: cheese proteins.

Then there’s the cheese.

Pecorino Romano contains proteins suspended in fat and moisture. As long as those proteins stay relatively loose, the cheese melts smoothly into the sauce. But once cheese gets too hot, those proteins tighten and bond together into dense tangled networks.

At roughly around 150°F to 160°F (65°C to 70°C), this process accelerates dramatically. Instead of dispersing smoothly into the sauce, the proteins seize into little clumps and strings while the fat separates away. This is why badly made cacio e pepe or carbonara often looks oily and stringy instead of creamy.

The extra-starchy water helps, to be sure, but it’s not a perfect safeguard. The only real way to control cheese clumping is to add the cheese off heat towards the very end, so that it doesn’t get a chance to begin clumping.

Finishing the Dish

Once you've got the sauce creamy and the cheese melted, it's ready to eat. All it needs is some hot bowls, extra cheese, pepper, and crisp guanciale for garnish, and mouths ready and waiting (it does not get better as it cools).

Turns out Carolina was right. Carbonara is not scrambled eggs and bacon, just like alla gricia is not merely pasta with pork and cheese. These dishes are technique disguised as simplicity: a little chemistry, a little heat control, and a little feel. Once you understand how fat, water, starch, and proteins come together in the pan, Roman pasta stops feeling like culinary magic and starts feeling like second nature. The difference between a greasy bowl of noodles and a glossy, silky sauce that clings perfectly to every strand isn’t some secret ingredient Romans are born knowing—it’s technique. And luckily for the rest of us, technique can be learned.

Recipe: Pasta Alla Gricia

What I love about this recipe:

  • It teaches foundational sauce technique instead of just giving you dinner.

  • It uses just a handful of ingredients, but rewards attention to detail.

  • Once you can make this, carbonara, cacio e pepe, and amatriciana are all within reach.

  • It’s one of the fastest paths I know to learning how restaurant-quality sauces actually work.

Yield: Serves 2
Active Time: 15 minutes
Total Time: 15 minutes
Notes: Use bronze die-extruded pasta brands, such as Rao’s or De Cecco. I like spaghetti or rigatoni. Guanciale has better fat distribution and a sharper flavor than pancetta, but pancetta (or even American-style bacon or salt pork) will work in its place.

Ingredients

For the Pasta

  • 8 ounces (225g) bronze-die extruded pasta, such as rigatoni, spaghetti, bucatini, or tonnarelli

  • Kosher salt

  • Pinch of MSG (optional)

  • 3 ounces (85g) guanciale (see note), cut into 1/4-inch- by 1/2-inch lardons

  • 1 teaspoon coarsely ground black pepper, plus more for serving

  • 2 ounces (55g) finely grated Pecorino Romano cheese, plus more for serving

Method

  1. Render the guanciale: Place the guanciale in a 12-inch skillet with about 2 tablespoons (30ml) water. Set over medium heat and cook, stirring occasionally, until the water evaporates and the guanciale becomes deeply browned and crisp, about 7 minutes. (Starting with water allows the fat to render gently before frying begins, preventing scorching and helping the pork cook evenly.) Once crisp, use a slotted spoon to remove the guanciale from the pan, leaving the fat behind.

  2. Bloom the black pepper: Add the black pepper cook for about 30 seconds, stirring constantly, until fragrant. Remove from heat and add a splash of water to cool the pan slightly and loosen browned bits from the bottom.

  3. Cook the pasta: Bring a wide skillet or sauté pan with about 1 1/2-inches of water to a boil. Add a modest amount of salt and, if desired, a pinch of MSG. Keep the seasoning lighter than usual because the pasta water will reduce later and become more concentrated. Add the pasta and cook until about 2 minutes shy of al dente. Reserve and set aside at least 2 cups (475ml) pasta water in a separate heat-proof vessel before draining the pasta and immediately adding it to the pan with the rendered guanciale.

  4. Build the emulsion: Set the pan over high heat and add 1/2 cup (120ml) of the reserved pasta water. Toss and stir constantly as the liquid reduces into a glossy sauce. Add more pasta water as needed while the pasta finishes cooking. (See troubleshooting guidelines below.)

  5. Add the cheese: When the pasta is cooked and the sauce is nice and creamy, remove from heat, then add about three-quarters of the Pecorino Romano and stir, toss, and shake vigorously until fully melted and emulsified. If the sauce tightens too much or begins clumping, add small splashes of pasta water until smooth again. Taste and adjust seasoning.

  6. Serve: Return most of the guanciale to the pan, reserving some for garnish. Give it a few good grinds of fresh black pepper. Toss to combine and taste and adjust for seasoning. Transfer to warm bowls and top with remaining Pecorino, crispy guanciale, and fresh black pepper.

Troubleshooting Emulsions

Roman pasta dishes are less about exact measurements than they are about reading the sauce as it develops. Here are the most common issues and how to fix them.

The Problem: The sauce looks greasy or broken

Your emulsion has started separating because there’s too much free fat relative to water and starch.

The Fix: Add a splash or two of pasta water and stir and toss aggressively over high heat to re-emulsify the sauce. The starch in the water will help pull the fat back into suspension.

The Problem: The sauce looks watery

Good. This is the easier problem.

The Fix: Just keep cooking. As water evaporates, the starch concentration increases and the sauce tightens naturally into a glossy glaze.

The Problem: The sauce looks perfect, but the pasta is still undercooked

This happens all the time.

The Fix: Add another splash of pasta water and keep cooking. You want enough liquid in the pan that the pasta can continue hydrating while the sauce repeatedly reduces and re-emulsifies around it. The goal is for the pasta and sauce to hit their perfect state at the same moment.

The Problem: The sauce was perfect in the pan but looks thick and clumpy on the plate

Your pasta probably cooled too quickly. Roman pasta sauces tighten as they cool because the cheese proteins and starches continue setting more firmly as they cool.

The Fix: Preheat your plates in a warm oven or toaster oven so that the pasta stays piping hot as you eat it.

The Problem: The cheese turns stringy

This happens when the cheese overheats.

The Fix: Well… there is no easy fix. Your best bet is to kill the heat completely, add a splash of pasta water, stir vigorously, and hope for the best. Typically once cheese proteins have entangled, there’s no turning back.
